topic: Teaching the manoeuvres: common errors, stall and spin demonstrations

notes.front: In the Flight Instructor for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, what is the Maneuver Lesson task?
notes.back: Area of Operation IV, Task A: a preflight lesson on a selected manoeuvre, presented as it would be taught to a student.
notes.explanation: The task tests ground instruction on a manoeuvre: the evaluator plays the student before any of the practical test is flown.
notes.example: Like the ground briefing an instructor gives before a steep-turn flight, but delivered to the evaluator as if to a student.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: The evaluator asks the applicant to present a preflight lesson on the selected maneuver as the lesson would be taught to a student and determines the outcome of this Task before the flight portion of the practical test.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the region of reversed command?
notes.back: The part of the power-required curve where additional power is needed to hold a slower airspeed.
notes.explanation: It lies on the slow side of the curve, where slowing down calls for more power rather than less.
notes.example: Like cycling into a headwind that grows as you slow: easing off does not rest you, and holding a slower pace takes more effort, not less.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: additional power is needed to maintain a slower airspeed. This

notes.front: The evaluator determines the outcome of the Maneuver Lesson task {{c1::before the flight portion}} of the practical test.
notes.back: before the flight portion
notes.explanation: It is a preflight lesson, presented on the ground as it would be taught to a student.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: The evaluator asks the applicant to present a preflight lesson on the selected maneuver as the lesson would be taught to a student and determines the outcome of this Task before the flight portion of the practical test.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May an applicant use lesson plans prepared before the practical test for the Maneuver Lesson task?
notes.back: Yes: previously developed lesson plans from the applicant's own library may be used.
notes.explanation: The note to Area of Operation IV permits it, so an applicant can bring a lesson plan already built for the manoeuvre.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: Previously developed lesson plans from the instructor applicant's library may be used.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For a single-engine land or sea applicant, from which Areas of Operation is the manoeuvre for the Maneuver Lesson selected?
notes.back: Areas of Operation VII through XII.
notes.explanation: Multi-engine land and sea applicants draw from a wider range, Areas VII through XIII.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: a maneuver Task selected from Area of Operation VII through Area of Operation XII (ASEL, ASES) or Area of Operation VII through Area of Operation XIII (AMEL, AMES)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The first knowledge element of the Maneuver Lesson task is the {{c1::purpose}} of the maneuver.
notes.back: purpose
notes.explanation: The applicant shows instructional knowledge by describing and explaining it, as a teacher would, not merely by knowing it.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: The applicant demonstrates instructional knowledge by describing and explaining: AI.IV.A.K1 Purpose of the maneuver.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The second knowledge element of the Maneuver Lesson task is the elements of the maneuver and the associated {{c1::common errors}}.
notes.back: common errors
notes.explanation: Elements and errors are paired in one element: the applicant teaches how the manoeuvre is flown and what commonly goes wrong in it.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: AI.IV.A.K2 Elements of the maneuver and the associated common errors.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The third knowledge element of the Maneuver Lesson task is the desired outcome(s), including {{c1::completion standards}}.
notes.back: completion standards
notes.explanation: Completion standards are part of the desired outcome the applicant describes and explains.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: AI.IV.A.K3 Desired outcome(s), including completion standards.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What risk must the applicant explain and teach in the Maneuver Lesson task?
notes.back: How to identify and manage the risk associated with the selected manoeuvre task.
notes.explanation: The applicant must both explain this risk and teach it.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: The applicant explains and teaches how to identify and manage risk associated with: AI.IV.A.R1 The selected maneuver Task.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the skill element of the Maneuver Lesson task require the applicant to do?
notes.back: Deliver instruction on the manoeuvre using a lesson plan, teaching methods and teaching aids, as appropriate, covering the three knowledge elements.
notes.explanation: The skill element turns the purpose, the elements and errors, and the desired outcomes into an actual lesson.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: Deliver instruction on the selected maneuver using a lesson plan, teaching methods, and teaching aids, as appropriate, that incorporate K1 through K3.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In integrated flight instruction, approximately {{c1::90}} percent of the pilot's attention should be devoted to outside visual references and scanning for airborne traffic.
notes.explanation: Attitude is controlled visually against the natural horizon, and the same outside view serves the scan for traffic.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-5
notes.evidence: The pilot visually controls the airplane's attitude in reference outside to the natural horizon. Approximately 90 percent of the pilot's attention should be devoted to outside visual references and scanning for airborne traffic.

notes.front: In integrated flight instruction, no more than about {{c1::10}} percent of the pilot's attention should be inside the flight deck.
notes.explanation: The pilot monitors performance by only briefly checking the flight instruments.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: The pilot should monitor the airplane's performance by briefly checking the flight instruments. No more than about 10 percent of the pilot's attention should be inside the flight deck.

notes.front: In integrated flight instruction, what job do the flight instruments do, and where is a correction applied?
notes.back: They validate attitude and confirm performance; the correction is applied with reference to the natural horizon.
notes.explanation: The instruments tell the pilot whether a correction is needed; the outside view is where it is made.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: The airplane's attitude is validated by referring to flight instruments and confirming performance. If the flight instruments display that the airplane's performance is in need of correction, the required correction needs to be determined and then precisely, smoothly, and accurately applied with reference to the natural horizon.

notes.front: Under integrated flight instruction, what does the handbook call the most common error of the beginner pilot?
notes.back: Making pitch or bank corrections while still looking inside.
notes.explanation: Fixating on the instruments is also common, and the beginner needs a conscious effort to return to outside references.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: The most common error made by the beginner pilot is to make pitch or bank corrections while still looking inside. It is also common for beginner pilots to fixate on the flight instruments—a conscious effort is required by them to return to outside visual references.

notes.front: What may a flight instructor use in the first several hours of instruction to stop a learner fixating on the instruments?
notes.back: Flight instrument covers, which force the use of outside visual references.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives the covers two uses: developing a beginner's skill and correcting a habit of fixating on instruments.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: For the first several hours of instruction, flight instructors may choose to use flight instrument covers to develop a beginning pilot's skill or to correct a pilot's poor habit of fixating on instruments by forcing them to use outside visual references for aircraft control.

notes.front: Why does a beginning pilot who flies attitude by the instruments invariably end up "chasing the instruments"?
notes.back: Not familiar with instrument lag and gyroscopic precession, the beginner makes excessive attitude corrections.
notes.explanation: The natural horizon, by contrast, gives immediate and accurate indications many times larger than any instrument.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: The beginning pilot, not being familiar with the intricacies of flight by references to instruments, including such things as instrument lag and gyroscopic precession, will invariably make excessive attitude corrections and end up "chasing the instruments." Airplane attitude by reference to the natural horizon, however, presents immediate and accurate indications many times larger than on any instrument.

notes.front: Why can a beginner miss a bank deviation that would be obvious outside the airplane?
notes.back: On the attitude indicator it may be imperceptible, though obvious against the wingtips or cowling and the natural horizon.
notes.explanation: The outside references show the same deviation large and plain; the instrument shows it only slightly.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: a deviation from a desired bank angle, which is obvious when referencing the airplane's wingtips or cowling relative to the natural horizon, may be imperceptible on the airplane's attitude indicator to the beginner pilot.

notes.front: If attitude cannot be established or maintained by reference to the natural horizon, the beginning pilot should understand that the situation has become {{c1::a genuine emergency}}.
notes.back: a genuine emergency
notes.explanation: Integrated flight instruction does not prepare pilots for flight in instrument meteorological conditions.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: anytime airplane attitude by reference to the natural horizon cannot be established or maintained, the situation has become a genuine emergency and that the use of integrated flight instruction does not prepare pilots for flight in IMC.

notes.front: A common straight-and-level error is forgetting the location of {{c1::preselected reference points}} on subsequent flights.
notes.back: preselected reference points
notes.explanation: The handbook lists it among the errors a learner shows when attitude is set against outside references from flight to flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: Forgetting the location of preselected reference points on subsequent flights.

notes.front: In straight-and-level flight, which common error involves the natural horizon?
notes.back: Trying to establish or correct attitude with the flight instruments rather than the natural horizon.
notes.explanation: The error is the reverse of integrated instruction, where attitude is set against the natural horizon.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: Attempting to establish or correct airplane attitude using flight instruments rather than the natural horizon.

notes.front: A common straight-and-level error is mechanically pushing or pulling on the flight controls rather than exerting {{c1::accurate and smooth pressure}}.
notes.back: accurate and smooth pressure
notes.explanation: The handbook contrasts moving the controls mechanically with applying pressure accurately and smoothly.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: Mechanically pushing or pulling on the flight controls rather than exerting accurate and smooth pressure.

notes.front: In straight-and-level flight, which common error concerns looking outside the aircraft?
notes.back: Not scanning outside for other traffic and for weather and terrain influences.
notes.explanation: The list names three things the outside scan is for: traffic, weather and terrain.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: Not scanning outside the aircraft for other traffic and weather and terrain influences.

notes.front: What does the handbook say a tight palm grip on the flight controls results in?
notes.back: A desensitised feeling in the hand and fingers.
notes.explanation: The grip is the error; the lost feel is its result.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: A tight palm grip on the flight controls resulting in a desensitized feeling of the hand and fingers.

notes.front: A common straight-and-level error is failure to make {{c1::timely and measured}} control inputs after a deviation from straight-and-level.
notes.back: timely and measured
notes.explanation: The error lies in the response to a deviation: late or unmeasured inputs.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: Failure to make timely and measured control inputs after a deviation from straight-and-level.

notes.front: What should be the pilot's primary reference for maintaining a level bank attitude?
notes.back: The wingtips.
notes.explanation: Watching only the nose's short horizontal reference line can let slight deviations go unnoticed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-8
notes.evidence: the nose's short horizontal reference line can cause slight deviations to go unnoticed. However, deviations from level flight are easily recognizable when the pilot references the wingtips and, as a result, the wingtips should be the pilot's primary reference for maintaining level bank attitude.

notes.front: What does the handbook say about a pilot with the habit of dragging one wing low and compensating with opposite rudder?
notes.back: The pilot will have difficulty mastering other flight manoeuvres.
notes.explanation: The handbook ties the habit to difficulty with other manoeuvres, not only straight-and-level flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-8
notes.evidence: A pilot with a bad habit of dragging one wing low and compensating with opposite rudder pressure will have difficulty mastering other flight maneuvers.

notes.front: In level turns, which common error concerns other traffic?
notes.back: Failing to clear adequately in the direction of turn.
notes.explanation: The clearing the handbook expects is specifically toward the side the airplane is turning.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Failure to adequately clear in the direction of turn for aircraft traffic.

notes.front: A common error in level turns is gaining or losing {{c1::altitude}} during the turn.
notes.back: altitude
notes.explanation: The item names a change of altitude in either direction as the error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Gaining or losing altitude during the turn.

notes.front: A common error in level turns is not holding the desired {{c1::bank angle}} constant.
notes.back: bank angle
notes.explanation: The item concerns holding the chosen bank, not choosing it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Not holding the desired bank angle constant.

notes.front: A common error in level turns is attempting to execute the turn solely by {{c1::instrument reference}}.
notes.back: instrument reference
notes.explanation: It mirrors the straight-and-level errors of flying attitude by instruments instead of outside references.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Attempting to execute the turn solely by instrument reference.

notes.front: Which level-turn error concerns the pilot's posture in the seat?
notes.back: Leaning away from the direction of the turn while seated.
notes.explanation: The list includes body position as well as control inputs.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Leaning away from the direction of the turn while seated.

notes.front: What does the handbook give as evidence of insufficient feel for the airplane in turns?
notes.back: Being unable to detect slips or skids without the flight instruments.
notes.explanation: Feel for the airplane is judged by whether uncoordinated flight is sensed without looking inside.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Insufficient feel for the airplane as evidenced by the inability to detect slips or skids without flight instruments.

notes.front: A common error in level turns is making skidding flat turns to avoid {{c1::banking the airplane}}.
notes.back: banking the airplane
notes.explanation: A flat turn uses rudder in place of bank, which the handbook describes as skidding.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Making skidding flat turns to avoid banking the airplane.

notes.front: A common error in level turns is holding excessive rudder in the {{c1::direction of turn}}.
notes.back: direction of turn
notes.explanation: It is one of several rudder and coordination faults in the list, alongside failing to coordinate the controls.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Holding excessive rudder in the direction of turn. 10. Gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction. 11. Failure to coordinate the controls.

notes.front: In climbs, which common error involves the airspeed indicator?
notes.back: Setting climb pitch attitude mainly by the airspeed indicator and chasing the airspeed.
notes.explanation: The item pairs the wrong primary reference with its result, chasing the airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Attempting to establish climb pitch attitude by primarily referencing the airspeed indicator and chasing the airspeed.

notes.front: A common climb error is applying elevator pressure too aggressively, resulting in {{c1::an excessive climb angle}}.
notes.back: an excessive climb angle
notes.explanation: The error is in how hard the elevator is applied at climb entry.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Applying elevator pressure too aggressively resulting in an excessive climb angle.

notes.front: In straight climbs, what does fixation on the airplane's nose result in?
notes.back: Climbing with one wing low.
notes.explanation: The fixation is on the nose; the handbook gives one wing low as the result.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Fixation on the airplane's nose during straight climbs, resulting in climbing with one wing low.

notes.front: What results from starting a climbing turn without coordinated use of the flight controls?
notes.back: No turn, and a climb with one wing low.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes the outcome: the intended turn does not happen.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Initiating a climbing turn without coordinated use of flight controls, resulting in no turn and a climb with one wing low.

notes.front: A common climbing-turn error is improper coordination resulting in a {{c1::slip}} that counteracts the rate of climb, giving little or no altitude gain.
notes.back: slip
notes.explanation: The slip works against the climb, so the airplane gains little or no altitude.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Improper coordination resulting in a slip that counteracts the rate of climb, resulting in little or no altitude gain.

notes.front: A common climbing-turn error is inability to keep {{c1::pitch and bank attitude}} constant.
notes.back: pitch and bank attitude
notes.explanation: Both axes need holding at once in a climbing turn, and the list names drifting in either.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Inability to keep pitch and bank attitude constant during climbing turns.

notes.front: What does excessive forward elevator pressure during level-off from a climb cause?
notes.back: A loss of altitude or excessive low G-force.
notes.explanation: The error happens at the end of the climb, in the transition to level flight.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Using excessive forward elevator pressure during level-off resulting in a loss of altitude or excessive low G-force.

notes.front: A common descent error is inadequate elevator back pressure during glide entry, resulting in {{c1::an overly steep glide}}.
notes.back: an overly steep glide
notes.explanation: The item links too little back pressure at glide entry to a glide steeper than intended.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Inadequate elevator back pressure during glide entry resulting in an overly steep glide.

notes.front: Entering a glide, what should the pilot do before lowering the pitch attitude?
notes.back: Slow the airplane to approximately glide speed.
notes.explanation: Lowering the nose before slowing to about glide speed is listed as a common error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Failure to slow the airplane to approximate glide speed prior to lowering pitch attitude.

notes.front: A common descent error is inability to sense changes in airspeed through {{c1::sound and feel}}.
notes.back: sound and feel
notes.explanation: The handbook expects the pilot to sense airspeed changes by sound and feel.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Inability to sense changes in airspeed through sound and feel.

notes.front: In descents, which common error involves back-elevator pressure to extend the glide?
notes.back: Attempting to "stretch" the glide by applying back-elevator pressure.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists the attempt itself as the error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Attempting to "stretch" the glide by applying back-elevator pressure.

notes.front: A common gliding-turn error is skidding or slipping and not recognising the difference in rudder forces {{c1::with and without power}}.
notes.back: with and without power
notes.explanation: Rudder needs in a glide differ from those under power, and missing the difference shows up as a slip or skid.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Skidding or slipping during gliding turns and not recognizing the difference in rudder forces with and without power.

notes.front: A common descent error is excessive {{c1::rudder}} pressure during recovery from gliding turns.
notes.back: rudder
notes.explanation: The list names rudder use on recovery from gliding turns as its own fault.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Excessive rudder pressure during recovery from gliding turns.

notes.front: Which gliding-turn error does the handbook tie specifically to flight near the ground?
notes.back: Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground.
notes.explanation: The list singles out cross-controlling when the gliding turn is made close to the ground.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground.

notes.front: Which common error opens the handbook's lists for normal, crosswind, short-field and soft-field takeoffs?
notes.back: Failure to review the POH and performance charts before takeoff.
notes.explanation: The error is made before the airplane moves: the review is due prior to takeoff.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Failure to review AFM/POH and performance charts prior to takeoff.

notes.front: In normal takeoffs, which common error concerns how the throttle is moved?
notes.back: Abrupt use of the throttle.
notes.explanation: The list names abruptness, not the amount of power, as the fault.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Abrupt use of the throttle. ⦁ Failure to check engine instruments for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power.

notes.front: A common normal-takeoff error is failure to check the {{c1::engine instruments}} for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power.
notes.back: engine instruments
notes.explanation: The item places the check right after takeoff power is applied.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Failure to check engine instruments for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power.

notes.front: What two common normal-takeoff errors concern the airplane's left turning tendency?
notes.back: Failing to anticipate it on initial acceleration; overcorrecting for it.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists both too little and too much response to the same tendency.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Failure to anticipate the airplane's left turning tendency on initial acceleration. ⦁ Overcorrecting for left turning tendency.

notes.front: A common normal-takeoff error is inadequate compensation for torque/P-factor during the initial climb, resulting in a {{c1::sideslip}}.
notes.back: sideslip
notes.explanation: The item names the result of the missing compensation: a sideslip.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Inadequate compensation for torque/P-factor during initial climb resulting in a sideslip.

notes.front: A common normal-takeoff error is over-control of the elevators during initial climb-out and lack of {{c1::elevator trimming}}.
notes.back: elevator trimming
notes.explanation: The list pairs over-controlling the elevator with not trimming it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Over-control of elevators during initial climb-out and lack of elevator trimming.

notes.front: After lift-off, what does limiting the scan to the area directly ahead of the airplane cause?
notes.back: A wing, usually the left, dropping immediately after lift-off.
notes.explanation: A scan limited to pitch attitude and direction ahead lets a wing drop; the handbook says usually the left.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Limiting scan to areas directly ahead of the airplane (pitch attitude and direction), causing a wing (usually the left) to drop immediately after lift-off.

notes.front: A common normal-takeoff error is failure to attain or maintain {{c1::best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY)}} or the desired climb airspeed.
notes.back: best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY)
notes.explanation: The item accepts either VY or the desired climb airspeed as the target.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Failure to attain/maintain best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY) or desired climb airspeed.

notes.front: A common crosswind-takeoff error is using less than {{c1::full aileron pressure}} into the wind initially on the takeoff roll.
notes.back: full aileron pressure
notes.explanation: The handbook expects full aileron into the wind at the start of the roll.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Crosswind Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-10
notes.evidence: Using less than full aileron pressure into the wind initially on the takeoff roll.

notes.front: In crosswind takeoffs, what should replace mechanical use of the aileron control?
notes.back: Judging lateral position on the runway from visual clues and applying enough aileron to stay centred.
notes.explanation: Aileron is set by what the pilot sees of the airplane's position on the runway, not by a fixed input.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Crosswind Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-10
notes.evidence: Mechanical use of aileron control rather than judging lateral position of airplane on runway from visual clues and applying sufficient aileron to keep airplane centered laterally on runway.

notes.front: A common crosswind-takeoff error is {{c1::side-skipping}} due to improper aileron application.
notes.back: side-skipping
notes.explanation: The handbook traces the side-skipping to the aileron, not the rudder.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Crosswind Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-10
notes.evidence: Side-skipping due to improper aileron application.

notes.front: What does excessive aileron input in the latter stage of the crosswind takeoff roll cause?
notes.back: A steep bank into the wind at lift-off.
notes.explanation: The error is made late in the roll and shows at lift-off as bank into the wind.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Crosswind Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-10
notes.evidence: Excessive aileron input in the latter stage of the takeoff roll resulting in a steep bank into the wind at lift-off.

notes.front: Which short-field takeoff error concerns setting up the airplane before the roll?
notes.back: Failure to have the airplane properly trimmed before takeoff.
notes.explanation: The item places the trim check before takeoff.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Failure to have the airplane properly trimmed prior to takeoff.

notes.front: A common short-field takeoff error is premature lift-off, resulting in {{c1::high drag}}.
notes.back: high drag
notes.explanation: Lifting off too early leaves the airplane in a high-drag state.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Premature lift-off resulting in high drag.

notes.front: A common short-field takeoff error is inadequate rotation, resulting in {{c1::excessive speed}} after lift-off.
notes.back: excessive speed
notes.explanation: The item links too little rotation to too much speed after lift-off.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Inadequate rotation resulting in excessive speed after lift-off. ⦁ Inability to attain/maintain VX.

notes.front: Which climb speed does the short-field takeoff error list name as one learners fail to attain or maintain?
notes.back: VX, the best angle of climb speed.
notes.explanation: The item names VX specifically for the short-field takeoff and maximum performance climb.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Inadequate rotation resulting in excessive speed after lift-off. ⦁ Inability to attain/maintain VX.

notes.front: A common short-field takeoff error is fixation on the {{c1::airspeed indicator}} during the initial climb.
notes.back: airspeed indicator
notes.explanation: The list names the fixation during the initial climb, just after lift-off.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Fixation on the airspeed indicator during initial climb.

notes.front: A common soft-field takeoff error is insufficient back-elevator pressure during the initial takeoff roll, resulting in inadequate {{c1::AOA}}.
notes.back: AOA (angle of attack)
notes.explanation: The error is in the first part of the roll, where the handbook expects back-elevator pressure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff and Climb, Common Errors, page 6-14
notes.evidence: Insufficient back-elevator pressure during initial takeoff roll resulting in inadequate AOA.

notes.front: Which soft-field takeoff error concerns the height flown just after lift-off?
notes.back: Climbing too high after lift-off and not levelling off low enough to hold the ground effect attitude.
notes.explanation: The handbook expects the airplane to stay low, in ground effect, after lift-off.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff and Climb, Common Errors, page 6-14
notes.evidence: Climbing too high after lift-off and not levelng off low enough to maintain ground effect attitude.

notes.front: A common soft-field takeoff error is {{c1::abrupt and/or excessive}} elevator control while trying to level off and accelerate after lift-off.
notes.back: abrupt and/or excessive
notes.explanation: The item places the error at the level-off to accelerate after lift-off.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff and Climb, Common Errors, page 6-14
notes.evidence: Abrupt and/or excessive elevator control while attempting to level off and accelerate after liftoff.

notes.front: A common soft-field takeoff error is failure to anticipate an increase in {{c1::pitch attitude}} as the airplane climbs out of ground effect.
notes.back: pitch attitude
notes.explanation: The list expects the pilot to foresee the pitch change on leaving ground effect.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff and Climb, Common Errors, page 6-14
notes.evidence: Failure to anticipate an increase in pitch attitude as the airplane climbs our of ground effect.

notes.front: A common normal-landing error is failure to complete the landing checklist {{c1::in a timely manner}}.
notes.back: in a timely manner
notes.explanation: The error is about timing: the checklist is done, but too late.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Failure to complete the landing checklist in a timely manner.

notes.front: In normal approaches, which common error concerns the base leg?
notes.back: Inadequate wind drift correction on the base leg.
notes.explanation: The next item in the list is a poorly judged turn onto final approach.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Inadequate wind drift correction on the base leg. 3. An overshooting, undershooting, too steep, or too shallow a turn onto final approach.

notes.front: What does the handbook give as the cause of a skidding turn from base leg to final approach?
notes.back: Overshooting, or inadequate wind drift correction.
notes.explanation: The skid is the result of an earlier error in the pattern, not a separate fault.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: A skidding turn from base leg to final approach as a result of overshooting/inadequate wind drift correction.

notes.front: A common normal-approach error is failure to adequately compensate for {{c1::flap extension}}.
notes.back: flap extension
notes.explanation: The list places it with unstable approaches and poor trim on final.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Unstable approach. 7. Failure to adequately compensate for flap extension. 8. Poor trim technique on final approach.

notes.front: A common normal-approach error is poor {{c1::trim technique}} on final approach.
notes.back: trim technique
notes.explanation: The handbook names trim technique on final as a separate item from flap compensation.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Poor trim technique on final approach.

notes.front: A common normal-landing error is touching down before attaining the proper {{c1::landing attitude}}.
notes.back: landing attitude
notes.explanation: The touchdown comes too early, before the attitude the landing needs.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Touching down prior to attaining proper landing attitude.

notes.front: Which common error appears in the handbook's lists for normal, crosswind, short-field and soft-field approaches and landings?
notes.back: Unstable approach.
notes.explanation: The same two words recur across the handbook's approach and landing error lists.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Poor coordination during turn from base to final approach. 6. Unstable approach.

notes.front: What should the flight instructor emphasise early on about go-arounds?
notes.back: That any approach or landing may result in a go-around.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it a fallacy that an aborted landing is always the result of a poor approach caused by lack of experience or skill.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: early on, and the pilot should understand, that any approach or landing may result in a go-around. The assumption that an aborted landing is invariably the consequence of a poor approach, which in turn is due to insufficient experience or skill, is a fallacy.

notes.front: What is the first common error in the handbook's list for go-arounds (rejected landings)?
notes.back: Failure to recognise a condition that warrants a rejected landing.
notes.explanation: The item is about recognising the condition, not about flying the go-around.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), Common Errors, page 9-12
notes.evidence: Failure to recognize a condition that warrants a rejected landing.

notes.front: The go-around is not inherently dangerous; it becomes dangerous only when {{c1::delayed unduly or executed improperly}}.
notes.back: delayed unduly or executed improperly
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that the most critical go-around is one started very close to the ground.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: the most critical go-around is one started when very close to the ground. The go-around maneuver is not inherently dangerous in itself. It becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or executed improperly.

notes.front: What does the handbook call the anticipatory belief that conditions are not as threatening as they are and that the approach is sure to end in a safe landing?
notes.back: Landing expectancy, or set: one of the two sources from which delay in starting a go-around normally stems.
notes.explanation: The belief is anticipatory: it settles the outcome of the approach before the landing is made.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: Landing expectancy or set—the anticipatory belief that conditions are not as threatening as they are and that the approach is sure to terminate with a safe landing.

notes.front: Which source of go-around delay is the mistaken belief that going around is an admission of failure?
notes.back: Pride.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the belief mistaken: going around does not admit failure to fly the approach properly.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: Pride—the mistaken belief that the act of going around is an admission of failure—failure to execute the approach properly.

notes.front: Which go-around error concerns how much power is applied and when?
notes.back: Failure to apply maximum allowable power in a timely manner.
notes.explanation: The item names two faults: less than maximum allowable power, or power applied late.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), Common Errors, page 9-12
notes.evidence: Failure to apply maximum allowable power in a timely manner.

notes.front: Why is abrupt power application a go-around error?
notes.back: Abrupt throttle movement makes the engine falter in some airplanes; power should go on smoothly and positively.
notes.explanation: The handbook wants the application smooth as well as positive, without hesitation.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: The application of power is smooth, as well as positive. Abrupt movements of the throttle in some airplanes cause the engine to falter.

notes.front: In a go-around at low altitude, what can allowing the nose to rise too early result in?
notes.back: An unrecoverable stall.
notes.explanation: Adding power suddenly tends to raise the nose, so the pilot should expect to need considerable forward elevator pressure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: The sudden addition of power tends to raise the airplane's nose and causes left yaw. Allowing the nose to rise too early could result in an unrecoverable stall when the go-around occurs at a low altitude. The pilot should anticipate the need for considerable forward elevator pressure

notes.front: In a go-around, what could a sudden and complete retraction of the flaps cause?
notes.back: A loss of lift, with the airplane settling into the ground.
notes.explanation: The handbook suggests raising them in small increments so the airplane can accelerate as they come up.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: it is wise to retract the flaps intermittently in small increments to allow time for the airplane to accelerate progressively as they are being raised. A sudden and complete retraction of the flaps could cause a loss of lift resulting in the airplane settling into the ground.

notes.front: A common forward-slip error is incorrect pitch adjustments that result in {{c1::poor airspeed control}}.
notes.back: poor airspeed control
notes.explanation: The error is named by its result: pitch adjusted wrongly shows up in airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Forward Slips to a Landing, Common Errors, page 9-15
notes.evidence: Incorrect pitch adjustments that result in poor airspeed control.

notes.front: Why can reacting to the airspeed indicator be an error in a slip?
notes.back: In some airplanes the pitot tube and static vent locations give considerable airspeed error in a slip.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to recognise a properly performed slip by attitude, the sound of the airflow and the feel of the controls.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Intentional Slips, page 9-13
notes.evidence: Because of the location of the pitot tube and static vents, airspeed indicators in some airplanes may have considerable error when the airplane is in a slip. The pilot needs to be aware of this possibility and recognize a properly performed slip by the attitude of the airplane, the sound of the airflow, and the feel of the flight controls.

notes.front: In a forward slip with a crosswind, which wing should the pilot lower?
notes.back: The upwind wing, so the airplane is banked into the crosswind.
notes.explanation: Slipping into the wind makes it easier to stay on the original flightpath.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Intentional Slips, page 9-13
notes.evidence: When a crosswind is present, the pilot should lower the upwind wing such that the airplane is banked into the crosswind since slipping into the wind makes it easier to remain on the original flightpath.

notes.front: When discontinuing a slip, what happens if rudder pressure is released abruptly?
notes.back: The nose swings into line too quickly and the airplane tends to gain excess speed.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to level the wings and release the rudder together while readjusting pitch to the normal glide attitude.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Intentional Slips, page 9-13
notes.evidence: Discontinuing a slip is accomplished by leveling the wings and simultaneously releasing the rudder pressure while readjusting the pitch attitude to the normal glide attitude. If the pressure on the rudder is released abruptly, the nose swings too quickly into line and the airplane tends to acquire excess speed.

notes.front: In crosswind landings, which common error concerns the turn from base leg to final?
notes.back: Undershooting or overshooting that turn.
notes.explanation: The list names both undershooting and overshooting in one item.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Undershooting or overshooting the turn from base leg to final approach.

notes.front: A common crosswind-landing error is inadequate compensation for {{c1::wind drift}} on final approach.
notes.back: wind drift
notes.explanation: The list names drift on final separately from drift at touchdown.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Inadequate compensation for wind drift on final approach.

notes.front: During a sideslip on crosswind final, what two effects can cause an excessive sink rate or too low an airspeed?
notes.back: Increased drag and reduced vertical lift.
notes.explanation: Both effects come from the sideslip itself; the list names their result in sink rate and airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Excessive sink rate or too low an airspeed from increased drag and reduced vertical lift during sideslip.

notes.front: A common crosswind-landing error is failure to apply appropriate {{c1::flight control inputs}} during rollout.
notes.back: flight control inputs
notes.explanation: The crosswind landing is not over at touchdown; the list continues into the rollout.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Failure to apply appropriate flight control inputs during rollout. 10. Failure to maintain direction control on rollout.

notes.front: Which short-field approach error concerns the shape of the final approach?
notes.back: A final approach that needs an overly steep approach and a high sink rate.
notes.explanation: The item is about how the final approach is set up.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Short-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-23
notes.evidence: A final approach that necessitates an overly steep approach and high sink rate.

notes.front: A common short-field approach error is undue delay in initiating {{c1::glide path corrections}}.
notes.back: glide path corrections
notes.explanation: The error is timing: the correction is right but late.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Short-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-23
notes.evidence: Undue delay in initiating glide path corrections.

notes.front: On short-field final, what does too low an airspeed result in?
notes.back: Inability to flare properly, and a hard landing.
notes.explanation: The item traces a hard landing back to the airspeed on final.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Short-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-23
notes.evidence: Too low an airspeed on final resulting in inability to flare properly and landing hard.

notes.front: A common short-field landing error is {{c1::excessive and/or unnecessary}} braking after touchdown.
notes.back: excessive and/or unnecessary
notes.explanation: The list names braking that is too hard or not needed at all.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Short-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-23
notes.evidence: Excessive and/or unnecessary braking after touchdown.

notes.front: A common soft-field approach error is excessive {{c1::descent rate}} on final approach.
notes.back: descent rate
notes.explanation: The item concerns the rate of descent on final, before the round out.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Soft-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-24
notes.evidence: Excessive descent rate on final approach.

notes.front: Why is excessive airspeed on a soft-field final an error?
notes.back: Higher approach speeds may cause excessive float in ground effect, which makes a smooth, controlled touchdown harder.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the short-field final-approach speed is equally appropriate to soft-field landings.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Soft-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-24
notes.evidence: The final-approach airspeed used for short-field landings is equally appropriate to soft-field landings. The use of higher approach speeds may result in excessive float in ground effect, and floating makes a smooth, controlled touchdown even more difficult.

notes.front: Which soft-field landing error concerns power in the round out and touchdown?
notes.back: Poor power management.
notes.explanation: The list names power handling in the round out and touchdown as its own error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Soft-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-24
notes.evidence: Poor power management during round out and touchdown.

notes.front: A common soft-field landing error is inadequate control of the airplane's weight transfer from {{c1::wings to wheels}} after touchdown.
notes.back: wings to wheels
notes.explanation: The error lies after touchdown, as the load moves from the wings onto the landing gear.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Soft-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-24
notes.evidence: Inadequate control of the airplane weight transfer from wings to wheels after touchdown.

notes.front: In power-off accuracy approaches, which common error concerns the spacing of the downwind leg?
notes.back: Flying the downwind leg too far from the runway or landing area.
notes.explanation: The list opens with where the downwind is flown, before any power-off glide begins.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, Common Errors, page 9-27
notes.evidence: Downwind leg is too far from the runway/landing area. 2. Overextension of downwind leg resulting from a tailwind.

notes.front: A common power-off accuracy approach error is inadequate compensation for wind drift on the {{c1::base leg}}.
notes.back: base leg
notes.explanation: The item moves from the downwind leg to drift on the base leg.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, Common Errors, page 9-27
notes.evidence: Overextension of downwind leg resulting from a tailwind. 3. Inadequate compensation for wind drift on base leg.

notes.front: In power-off accuracy approaches, why does the handbook say pilots make skidding turns?
notes.back: In an effort to increase gliding distance.
notes.explanation: The skid is listed as an error along with its motive.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, Common Errors, page 9-27
notes.evidence: Skidding turns in an effort to increase gliding distance.

notes.front: A common power-off accuracy approach error in retractable-gear airplanes is failure to lower the {{c1::landing gear}}.
notes.back: landing gear
notes.explanation: The list names the gear only for airplanes that have retractable gear.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, Common Errors, page 9-27
notes.evidence: Failure to lower landing gear in retractable gear airplanes.

notes.front: Which throttle error does the handbook list for power-off accuracy approaches?
notes.back: Using the throttle to increase the glide instead of merely clearing the engine.
notes.explanation: The item contrasts increasing the glide with merely clearing the engine.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, Common Errors, page 9-27
notes.evidence: Use of throttle to increase the glide instead of merely clearing the engine.

notes.front: Why should a pilot never try to stretch a glide to reach the landing spot?
notes.back: With pitch raised too high, the airplane settles rapidly from slow airspeed and insufficient lift.
notes.explanation: The handbook states the rapid settling as its reason for the rule.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, page 9-25
notes.evidence: If the pitch attitude is raised too high, the airplane settles rapidly due to a slow airspeed and insufficient lift. For this reason, the pilot should never try to stretch a glide to reach the desired landing spot.

notes.front: In a power-off accuracy approach, when should full flaps be added?
notes.back: Only once it is clear that adding them will not cause the landing to be short of the point.
notes.explanation: The handbook also says never to retract the flaps to reach the spot.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, 90° Power-Off Approach, page 9-26
notes.evidence: Full flaps should be delayed until it is clear that adding them will not cause the landing to be short of the point. The pilot should never try to stretch the glide or retract the flaps to reach the desired landing spot.

notes.front: A flight instructor applicant's Maneuver Lesson on short-field landings explains why the manoeuvre is flown, how each step is performed and the completion standards, but never mentions what learners tend to get wrong. Which knowledge element is incomplete?
notes.back: C) The elements of the manoeuvre and the associated common errors
notes.choices:
A) The desired outcomes, including completion standards
B) The purpose of the manoeuvre
C) The elements of the manoeuvre and the associated common errors
D) None: common errors belong only to the flight portion
notes.choicesExplained: B: the lesson explains why the manoeuvre is flown. A: the completion standards are covered. D: the second knowledge element pairs the elements with their common errors, taught in the preflight lesson.
notes.explanation: The Maneuver Lesson pairs the manoeuvre's elements with its common errors in one knowledge element, so leaving out the errors leaves it incomplete.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation IV, Task A. Maneuver Lesson, page 26
notes.evidence: AI.IV.A.K2 Elements of the maneuver and the associated common errors.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On an early lesson, a learner in level flight notices the attitude indicator showing a slight bank, then rolls the wings level while still staring at the instrument. What should the instructor coach?
notes.back: D) Check the instrument briefly, then make the correction looking outside against the natural horizon
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: correcting on the instrument is more precise for a beginner
B) Make the correction by the instrument, then look outside to scan for traffic
C) Stop checking instruments altogether and fly only by outside references
D) Check the instrument briefly, then make the correction looking outside against the natural horizon
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook names corrections made while still looking inside as the beginner's most common error. C: integrated instruction still uses the instruments to validate attitude and confirm performance. B: the correction itself belongs outside, against the natural horizon.
notes.explanation: Correcting while still looking inside is the most common beginner error under integrated flight instruction.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: The most common error made by the beginner pilot is to make pitch or bank corrections while still looking inside.

notes.front: A student pilot trained only by integrated flight instruction flies into cloud and loses sight of the natural horizon. How should the instructor have taught the student to regard this?
notes.back: C) As a genuine emergency, for which integrated instruction does not prepare the pilot
notes.choices:
A) As routine, because integrated instruction teaches flight by instruments
B) As a minor distraction, to be handled by switching to 90 percent instrument attention
C) As a genuine emergency, for which integrated instruction does not prepare the pilot
D) As a cue to chase the flight instruments until the horizon reappears
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says integrated instruction does not prepare pilots for flight in instrument meteorological conditions. B: the 90 percent figure is for outside references, and losing the horizon is called a genuine emergency. D: chasing the instruments is itself a beginner error the handbook describes.
notes.explanation: The handbook tells the beginning pilot that losing the natural horizon as an attitude reference makes the situation a genuine emergency.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Integrated Flight Instruction, page 3-6
notes.evidence: anytime airplane attitude by reference to the natural horizon cannot be established or maintained, the situation has become a genuine emergency and that the use of integrated flight instruction does not prepare pilots for flight in IMC.

notes.front: In cruise a learner holds heading, but the left wing is always slightly low and the learner keeps light right rudder to stop the turn. Which common error is this?
notes.back: D) Habitually flying with one wing low or keeping direction with the rudder alone
notes.choices:
A) Forgetting preselected reference points on later flights
B) Leaning away from the direction of turn
C) Mechanically pushing or pulling on the controls
D) Habitually flying with one wing low or keeping direction with the rudder alone
notes.choicesExplained: A: the problem is bank, not where the reference points are. B: that is a level-turn error about the pilot's posture. C: the inputs here are steady, not mechanical; the fault is the wing-low habit.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists habitually flying one wing low, or holding direction with rudder only, as a straight-and-level error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: Habitually flying with one wing low or maintaining directional control using only the rudder control.

notes.front: A learner told to hold altitude watches the altimeter and vertical speed indicator, answering every needle movement with a new pitch input, and the airplane porpoises. Which common error best describes this?
notes.back: C) "Chasing" the flight instruments rather than attitude flying
notes.choices:
A) Not scanning outside for traffic
B) A tight palm grip on the controls
C) "Chasing" the flight instruments rather than attitude flying
D) Forgetting preselected reference points
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing suggests a desensitised grip; the fault is where the learner is looking. A: the learner may also be neglecting the lookout, but that does not cause the porpoising, which comes from following the needles. D: the learner is not using outside references at all.
notes.explanation: Following each needle movement instead of holding an attitude is what the handbook calls chasing the instruments.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Straight-and-Level Flight, Common Errors, page 3-9
notes.evidence: "Chasing" the flight instruments rather than adhering to the principles of attitude flying.

notes.front: Through a 30° turn a learner keeps the nose's position on the horizon fixed and never glances at the wingtips; the bank slowly steepens. Which common error does this show?
notes.back: C) Trying to hold a constant bank by referencing only the airplane's nose
notes.choices:
A) Failure to clear in the direction of turn
B) Holding excessive rudder in the direction of turn
C) Trying to hold a constant bank by referencing only the airplane's nose
D) Gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing in the scenario concerns clearing for traffic. B: no rudder fault is described. D: the scenario is about bank reference, not training balance.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists holding bank by the nose alone as a level-turn error; the nose gives a poor reference for bank.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Attempting to maintain a constant bank angle by referencing only the airplane's nose.

notes.front: A learner flies tidy turns to the left but loses altitude and bank control in every turn to the right. The logbook shows almost all practice has been left turns. Which common error is the instructor seeing?
notes.back: D) Gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction
notes.choices:
A) Leaning away from the direction of turn
B) Making skidding flat turns to avoid banking
C) Attempting to turn solely by instrument reference
D) Gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction
notes.choicesExplained: A: posture is not described; the pattern follows turn direction. B: the learner does bank; the weakness is in one direction. C: nothing suggests instrument fixation.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists proficiency gained in turns in only one direction as a level-turn error in its own right.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Level Turns, Common Errors, page 3-17
notes.evidence: Gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction.

notes.front: Climbing straight ahead after takeoff in a single-engine airplane, a learner keeps the wings level but the nose slowly yaws left. What is the most likely cause, by the handbook's list?
notes.back: A) Inadequate right rudder pressure
notes.choices:
A) Inadequate right rudder pressure
B) Excessive forward elevator at level-off
C) Fixation on the nose, giving one wing low
D) Applying elevator pressure too aggressively
notes.choicesExplained: D: that gives an excessive climb angle, not yaw. B: the airplane is still climbing. C: the wings are level; the fault is yaw.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists yaw during climbs, usually due to inadequate right rudder pressure, as a common error; it says "usually", so it is the likeliest cause, not the only one.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, Common Errors, page 3-20
notes.evidence: Allowing the airplane to yaw during climbs usually due to inadequate right rudder pressure.

notes.front: At full climb power a learner insists on matching the climb rate seen on an earlier flight and keeps raising the nose as the airspeed decays. What limits the climb rate the learner is trying to exceed?
notes.back: D) The excess thrust available
notes.choices:
A) The pilot's rate of elevator input
B) The elevator authority available
C) Only the trim setting
D) The excess thrust available
notes.choicesExplained: B: raising the nose further does not add thrust to offset drag. C: trim relieves control pressure; it does not supply thrust. A: the handbook ties climb rate to excess thrust, not to how the elevator is moved.
notes.explanation: A climb is sustained only while thrust offsets the extra drag, which caps the climb rate.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Climbs and Climbing Turns, page 3-17
notes.evidence: An airplane can only sustain a climb when there is sufficient thrust to offset increased drag; therefore, climb rate is limited by the excess thrust available.

notes.front: In a straight glide a learner watches the airspeed indicator, raising the nose whenever the needle rises and lowering it whenever it falls; the glide never settles. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Inability to stabilise the glide, chasing the airspeed indicator
notes.choices:
A) Cross-controlling near the ground
B) Inability to stabilise the glide, chasing the airspeed indicator
C) Failure to slow to glide speed before lowering pitch
D) Excessive rudder during gliding-turn recovery
notes.choicesExplained: A: no cross-controlling is described. C: the entry is complete; the problem is holding the glide. D: the glide is straight.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes chasing the airspeed indicator as the inability to stabilise the glide.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Inability to stabilize the glide (chasing the airspeed indicator).

notes.front: From a stable glide a learner rolls into a gliding turn but holds the same pitch attitude as in the straight glide. What does the handbook say follows?
notes.back: A) A decrease in airspeed
notes.choices:
A) A decrease in airspeed
B) No change, as long as bank stays constant
C) An increase in airspeed
D) An overly steep glide
notes.choicesExplained: C: the handbook links this error to a decrease in airspeed. B: failing to lower pitch at gliding-turn entry is itself listed as causing a speed loss. D: that follows too little back pressure at glide entry, a different error.
notes.explanation: Failing to lower pitch attitude when entering a gliding turn is listed as a common error because airspeed decreases.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 3, Descents and Descending Turns, Common Errors, page 3-24
notes.evidence: Failure to lower pitch attitude during gliding turn entry resulting in a decrease in airspeed.

notes.front: On the takeoff roll a learner stares at the airspeed indicator and rotates only when the needle reaches the rotation speed, paying no attention to how the controls feel or what the runway looks like. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Relying solely on the airspeed indicator instead of visual references and tracking clues
notes.choices:
A) Abrupt use of the throttle
B) Relying solely on the airspeed indicator instead of visual references and tracking clues
C) Lack of elevator trimming in the climb
D) Overcorrecting for left turning tendency
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing is said about how power was applied. D: no directional fault is described. C: the airplane has not yet lifted off.
notes.explanation: The handbook wants the learner to develop an understanding of visual references and tracking clues of airspeed and controllability, not to rely only on the indicator.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Normal Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-6
notes.evidence: Relying solely on the airspeed indicator rather than developing an understanding of visual references and tracking clues of airplane airspeed and controllability during acceleration and lift-off.

notes.front: With the wind from the left, a learner lifts off cleanly but then lets the airplane drift right of the extended runway centreline. Which common crosswind-takeoff error is this?
notes.back: D) Inadequate drift correction after lift-off
notes.choices:
A) Using less than full aileron at the start of the roll
B) Side-skipping due to improper aileron
C) Excessive aileron late in the roll
D) Inadequate drift correction after lift-off
notes.choicesExplained: B: side-skipping happens on the runway, before lift-off. C: that gives a steep bank into the wind at lift-off, not drift afterwards. A: the lift-off was clean; the fault comes after it.
notes.explanation: The handbook's crosswind-takeoff list ends with inadequate drift correction once airborne.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Crosswind Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-10
notes.evidence: Excessive aileron input in the latter stage of the takeoff roll resulting in a steep bank into the wind at lift-off. ⦁ Inadequate drift correction after lift-off.

notes.front: For a short-field takeoff a learner taxis onto the runway at a mid-field intersection, leaving a third of the runway behind the airplane. Which common error is this?
notes.back: C) Failure to use all available runway
notes.choices:
A) Premature lift-off resulting in high drag
B) Failure to have the airplane properly trimmed
C) Failure to use all available runway
D) Premature retraction of the flaps
notes.choicesExplained: A: the airplane has not begun the roll. B: trim is not described. D: that happens after lift-off.
notes.explanation: The short-field list names failing to use all available runway or takeoff area.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Failure to utilize all available runway/takeoff area.

notes.front: Seconds after a short-field lift-off, with the obstacle still ahead, a learner reaches for the flap lever and raises the flaps. Which common error is this?
notes.back: D) Premature retraction of wing flaps
notes.choices:
A) Inadequate rotation
B) Holding the airplane on the ground with forward elevator
C) Failure to review the performance charts
D) Premature retraction of wing flaps
notes.choicesExplained: A: the airplane has already lifted off and is climbing. B: the airplane is airborne. C: the fault is an action in the climb, not preparation.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists premature retraction of landing gear or flaps among short-field takeoff errors.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Premature retraction of landing gear and/or wing flaps.

notes.front: On a soft-field takeoff the airplane lifts off at low speed and the learner immediately pitches up for a normal climb. Which common error is this?
notes.back: C) Climbing out of ground effect before reaching sufficient climb speed
notes.choices:
A) Insufficient back-elevator pressure on the initial roll
B) Poor directional control
C) Climbing out of ground effect before reaching sufficient climb speed
D) Failure to cross-check the engine instruments
notes.choicesExplained: A: the fault comes after lift-off. B: no directional problem is described. D: the fault is the pitch-up, not the engine check.
notes.explanation: The soft-field list names climbing out of the ground effect area before sufficient climb speed is reached.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff and Climb, Common Errors, page 6-14
notes.evidence: Attempting to climb our of ground effect area before attaining sufficient climb speed.

notes.front: Just after a soft-field lift-off, the learner relaxes back pressure too much and the airplane sinks until the wheels touch the surface again. Which common error is this?
notes.back: C) Allowing the airplane to "mush" or settle, giving an inadvertent touchdown
notes.choices:
A) Failure to anticipate a pitch increase leaving ground effect
B) Climbing too high after lift-off
C) Allowing the airplane to "mush" or settle, giving an inadvertent touchdown
D) Failure to review the performance charts
notes.choicesExplained: B: the airplane went down, not up. A: the airplane never left ground effect. D: the fault is in the handling after lift-off.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists letting the airplane mush or settle after lift-off, ending in an inadvertent touchdown.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff and Climb, Common Errors, page 6-14
notes.evidence: Allowing the airplane to "mush" or settle resulting in an inadvertant touchdown after lift-off.

notes.front: Low on final with power at idle, a learner raises the nose to hold altitude and "reach" the runway, without adding power. Which common error is this?
notes.back: A) Trying to maintain altitude or reach the runway using elevator alone
notes.choices:
A) Trying to maintain altitude or reach the runway using elevator alone
B) Poor trim technique on final
C) Failure to compensate for flap extension
D) Excessive braking after touchdown
notes.choicesExplained: B: the fault is using the elevator in place of power, not trim. C: no flap change is described. D: the airplane is still on final.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists using the elevator alone to hold altitude or reach the runway as a normal-approach error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Attempting to maintain altitude or reach the runway using elevator alone.

notes.front: After a good touchdown in a nosewheel airplane, a learner lets go of the back pressure at once and the nosewheel slams onto the runway. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Failure to hold sufficient back-elevator pressure after touchdown
notes.choices:
A) Touching down before the proper landing attitude
B) Failure to hold sufficient back-elevator pressure after touchdown
C) Focusing too far ahead, giving a low round out
D) Excessive braking after touchdown
notes.choicesExplained: A: the touchdown was good; the fault came after it. C: the round out is not the problem. D: no braking is described.
notes.explanation: The normal-landing list includes failing to hold enough back-elevator pressure once on the ground.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Failure to hold sufficient back-elevator pressure after touchdown.

notes.front: A learner starts a go-around a few feet above the runway and, feeling the airplane float, pitches straight up to the climb attitude. What does the handbook warn may happen?
notes.back: B) The airplane may be unable to climb, or even hold altitude, at full power
notes.choices:
A) The airplane climbs better, because ground effect adds lift
B) The airplane may be unable to climb, or even hold altitude, at full power
C) The engine falters from the pitch change
D) Nothing, provided full power is set
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook calls the ground-effect "cushion of air" imaginary and the extra performance "borrowed". D: the warning applies even at full power. C: faltering is linked to abrupt throttle movement, not pitch.
notes.explanation: Close to the ground the handbook asks the pilot to factor in ground effect, and warns against climbing prematurely.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), Ground Effect, page 9-12
