notes.evidence: The pilot needs to factor in ground effect when initiating a go-around close to the ground. An attempt to climb prematurely may result in the airplane not being able to climb or even maintain altitude at full power.

notes.front: During a go-around a learner applies full power and holds the attitude, but the nose yaws left and the ball swings out. What has the learner not done?
notes.back: D) Applied enough right rudder to counteract torque and P-factor
notes.choices:
A) Retracted the landing gear before the flaps
B) Retracted the flaps fully at once
C) Reduced power to stop the yaw
D) Applied enough right rudder to counteract torque and P-factor
notes.choicesExplained: B: sudden full retraction risks a loss of lift, not yaw. C: maximum allowable power is held in a go-around. A: the order of retraction does not explain yaw.
notes.explanation: Right rudder is how the handbook has the pilot counter torque and P-factor in the go-around.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Go-Arounds (Rejected Landings), page 9-11
notes.evidence: The pilot applies sufficient right rudder pressure to counteract torque and P-factor.

notes.front: High on final, a learner sets up a forward slip to lose height but leaves the power at the setting used for the normal descent. What should the instructor correct?
notes.back: B) Reduce the power, normally to idle, to use the slip to lose altitude
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: power has no effect on a slip
B) Reduce the power, normally to idle, to use the slip to lose altitude
C) Add power so the airspeed stays up
D) Lower the downwind wing
notes.choicesExplained: A: using excess power while trying to lose altitude is a listed forward-slip error. C: airspeed in the slip is controlled with the elevator. D: the upwind wing is lowered, and the fault here is power.
notes.explanation: For altitude loss in a forward slip, power is normally at idle, with airspeed held by the elevator.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Intentional Slips, page 9-13
notes.evidence: In order to use the maneuver to lose altitude, power is normally reduced to idle. The pilot controls airspeed using elevator control.

notes.front: With a crosswind from the right, a learner forward slips on final by lowering the left wing. Which common error is this?
notes.back: D) A slip in the same direction as the crosswind
notes.choices:
A) Reacting to erroneous airspeed indications
B) Using excess power while losing altitude
C) Incorrect pitch adjustments
D) A slip in the same direction as the crosswind
notes.choicesExplained: A: the fault is the direction of the slip, not the airspeed reading. B: power is not described. C: pitch is not described.
notes.explanation: Lowering the left wing with wind from the right slips with the crosswind, which the handbook lists as an error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Forward Slips to a Landing, Common Errors, page 9-15
notes.evidence: A slip in the same direction as any crosswind.

notes.front: A learner flies a crab down final and is still crabbed when the wheels touch, the nose pointing well left of the runway. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Failure to touch down with the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway
notes.choices:
A) Excessive airspeed on touchdown
B) Failure to touch down with the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway
C) Excessive braking
D) Undershooting the turn to final
notes.choicesExplained: A: speed is not described. D: the fault is at touchdown, not the turn to final. C: no braking is described.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists touching down with the longitudinal axis not aligned with the runway.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Failure to touch down with the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway.

notes.front: The crosswind component is well above the value the POH gives as demonstrated, and a learner wants to land anyway "for the practice". What does the handbook list this as?
notes.back: D) A common error: attempting a landing in crosswinds exceeding the maximum demonstrated crosswind component
notes.choices:
A) A go-around error
B) Acceptable, since the demonstrated value is only advisory
C) A risk only if the runway is short
D) A common error: attempting a landing in crosswinds exceeding the maximum demonstrated crosswind component
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook lists the attempt itself as a common error. C: runway length is not part of the listed error. A: it is listed among crosswind approach and landing errors.
notes.explanation: The crosswind-landing error list begins with attempting to land beyond the maximum demonstrated crosswind component.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Attempted landing in crosswinds that exceed the airplane's maximum demonstrated crosswind component.

notes.front: On a crosswind landing the airplane is aligned with the centreline, but it is moving sideways across the runway as the wheels touch. Which common error is this?
notes.back: C) Touching down while drifting
notes.choices:
A) Failure to align the longitudinal axis
B) Excessive airspeed on touchdown
C) Touching down while drifting
D) Loss of directional control on rollout
notes.choicesExplained: A: the airplane is aligned; it is moving sideways. B: speed is not described. D: the fault happens at touchdown, before the rollout.
notes.explanation: Alignment and drift are listed separately: the airplane can be aligned yet still drifting.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Crosswind Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-20
notes.evidence: Failure to touch down with the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway. 7. Touching down while drifting.

notes.front: A learner flies the short-field final well above the recommended approach speed and floats far past the aiming point in the round out. Which common error is this?
notes.back: C) Too high an airspeed, resulting in floating on round out
notes.choices:
A) Too low an airspeed, giving a hard landing
B) Undue delay in glide path corrections
C) Too high an airspeed, resulting in floating on round out
D) Excessive braking after touchdown
notes.choicesExplained: A: the speed is too high, not too low. B: the float comes from speed, not a late correction. D: the airplane has not touched down.
notes.explanation: Excess speed on a short-field final shows up as floating on round out.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Short-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-23
notes.evidence: Too high an airspeed resulting in floating on round out.

notes.front: On a short-field landing a learner closes the throttle to idle as soon as the round out begins, and the airplane drops onto the runway. Which common error is this?
notes.back: A) Prematurely reducing power to idle on round out
notes.choices:
A) Prematurely reducing power to idle on round out
B) Failure to maintain directional control
C) A final approach that is overly steep
D) Too high an airspeed on final
notes.choicesExplained: D: the airplane dropped rather than floated. B: no directional problem is described. C: the fault is in the round out, not the final approach.
notes.explanation: The handbook links a premature power reduction on round out to a hard landing.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Short-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-23
notes.evidence: Prematurely reducing power to idle on round out resulting in hard landing.

notes.front: On a grass-strip landing a learner touches down on the main wheels, then releases back pressure so the nosewheel drops onto the surface. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Allowing the nosewheel to "fall" rather than controlling its descent
notes.choices:
A) Round out too high above the surface
B) Allowing the nosewheel to "fall" rather than controlling its descent
C) Excessive descent rate on final
D) Excessive airspeed on final
notes.choicesExplained: A: the round out is not described. C: the fault comes after touchdown. D: speed is not described.
notes.explanation: The soft-field list ends with letting the nosewheel fall to the runway instead of controlling its descent.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Soft-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-24
notes.evidence: Allowing the nose-wheel to "fall" to the runway after touchdown rather than controlling its descent.

notes.front: Landing on a soft strip, a learner starts the flare at about twice the normal height and holds the airplane off well above the surface. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Round out too high above the runway surface
notes.choices:
A) Poor power management during round out
B) Round out too high above the runway surface
C) Inadequate weight transfer control after touchdown
D) Allowing the nosewheel to fall
notes.choicesExplained: A: power is not described. C: the airplane has not touched down. D: the airplane is still airborne.
notes.explanation: The soft-field list names rounding out too high above the runway surface.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Soft-Field Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-24
notes.evidence: Round out too high above the runway surface.

notes.front: On a 180° power-off approach a learner sees the airplane will float past the chosen spot and pushes the nose down to plant it on the spot. What does the handbook prefer?
notes.back: B) A good landing beyond the spot rather than a poor one on or just past it
notes.choices:
A) Forcing the airplane on so the spot is achieved
B) A good landing beyond the spot rather than a poor one on or just past it
C) Adding power to extend the float
D) Retracting the flaps to stretch the float
notes.choicesExplained: A: forcing the airplane onto the runway to avoid overshooting is a listed error. C: using throttle to change the glide is also a listed error. D: the handbook says never to retract the flaps to reach the spot.
notes.explanation: On short final, the handbook puts a good, safe landing ahead of hitting the selected spot.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, 90° Power-Off Approach, page 9-26
notes.evidence: On short final, full attention is given to making a good, safe landing rather than concentrating on the selected landing spot. The approach angle used and final approach airspeed determine the probability of landing on the spot, and late adjustments to these parameters are not appropriate. It is always better to execute a good landing away from the spot

notes.front: On a 180° power-off approach the wind is blowing along the downwind leg in the direction of flight, and the learner flies the downwind as if the wind were calm, ending up far beyond the usual abeam point. Which common error is this?
notes.back: B) Overextension of the downwind leg resulting from a tailwind
notes.choices:
A) Downwind leg too far from the runway
B) Overextension of the downwind leg resulting from a tailwind
C) Premature flap extension
D) Skidding turns to extend the glide
notes.choicesExplained: A: the fault is the length of the downwind, not its distance from the runway. D: no turn is described. C: flaps are not described.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists overextending the downwind because of a tailwind as a power-off accuracy approach error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Power-Off Accuracy Approaches, Common Errors, page 9-27
notes.evidence: Overextension of downwind leg resulting from a tailwind.

notes.front: In a normal landing, how does where the pilot focuses affect round-out height?
notes.back: Focusing too close to the airplane gives a too high round out; too far gives a too low one.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists the two as a pair of opposite errors with opposite results.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 9, Normal Approach and Landing, Common Errors, page 9-10
notes.evidence: Focusing too close to the airplane resulting in a too high round out. 11. Focusing too far from the airplane resulting in a too low round out.

notes.front: On the takeoff roll, how do the elevator errors listed for short-field and soft-field takeoffs differ?
notes.back: Short-field: holding the airplane on the ground with excessive forward elevator. Soft-field: insufficient back-elevator pressure on the initial roll.
notes.explanation: The two lists name opposite elevator faults for the ground roll.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 6, Short-Field and Soft/Rough-Field Takeoff, Common Errors, page 6-12
notes.evidence: Holding the airplane on the ground unnecessarily with excessive forward-elevator pressure.

notes.front: For rectangular courses, turns around a point, S-turns and eights on pylons, each handbook list of common errors opens with failing to {{c1::adequately clear the surrounding area for safety hazards}}.
notes.back: adequately clear the surrounding area for safety hazards
notes.explanation: The handbook adds “initially and throughout the maneuver”, so the lookout covers the whole manoeuvre. For eights on pylons, the list comes after the rudder error the handbook calls most common.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Rectangular Course”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: Failure to adequately clear the surrounding area for safety hazards, initially and throughout the maneuver.

notes.front: In the handbook lists for rectangular courses, turns around a point and S-turns, which altitude error happens before the manoeuvre starts?
notes.back: Failing to establish a constant, level altitude before entering the manoeuvre.
notes.explanation: The lists give holding altitude during the manoeuvre as a separate item, so the entry and the manoeuvre itself are judged apart.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Rectangular Course”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: Failure to establish a constant, level altitude prior to entering the maneuver. 3. Failure to maintain altitude during the maneuver.

notes.evidence: Failure to properly trim the airplane 10. Failure to respond to a stall warning Stalls

notes.front: Both the handbook’s slow-flight and intentional-stall lists open with failing to {{c1::adequately clear the area}}.
notes.back: adequately clear the area
notes.explanation: Clearing heads both lists, as it heads the ground-reference and performance-manoeuvre lists.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Common errors in the performance of intentional stalls are: 1. Failure to adequately clear the area.

notes.front: Which intentional-stall error involves over-relying on two instruments after recovery?
notes.back: Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues.
notes.explanation: The fault is not using the instruments but excluding the other cues while doing so.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery.

notes.front: During a power-off or power-on stall entry, what does pulling too fast on the controls cause?
notes.back: An inadvertent accelerated stall.
notes.explanation: The handbook names the unintended result, an accelerated stall, inside the error itself.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on the controls during a power-off or power-on stall entry.

notes.front: Which intentional-stall error concerns recognising that a stall is near?
notes.back: Inability to recognise an impending stall condition.
notes.explanation: The next item, failing to act in time during impending stalls, follows on from recognising one.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Inability to recognize an impending stall condition. 5. Failure to take timely action to prevent a full stall during the conduct of impending stalls.

notes.front: When practising impending stalls, which error does the handbook list?
notes.back: Failing to take timely action to prevent a full stall.
notes.explanation: It comes after inability to recognise an impending stall: recognising it is not enough without prompt action.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Inability to recognize an impending stall condition. 5. Failure to take timely action to prevent a full stall during the conduct of impending stalls.

notes.front: Which intentional-stall error applies to turning stalls?
notes.back: Failing to maintain a constant bank angle.
notes.explanation: The list limits this item to turning stalls, where a bank angle is set.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls.

notes.front: Which intentional-stall error concerns the rudder throughout the stall and recovery?
notes.back: Failing to maintain proper coordination with the rudder.
notes.explanation: The handbook covers the whole sequence, not just the entry: “throughout the stall and recovery”.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Failure to maintain proper coordination with the rudder throughout the stall and recovery.

notes.front: When practising the full stall, which error involves the critical AOA?
notes.back: Recovering before reaching the critical AOA.
notes.explanation: The item applies only when practising the full stall manoeuvre.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Recovering before reaching the critical AOA when practicing the full stall maneuver.

notes.front: Which intentional-stall error involves automation?
notes.back: Not disconnecting the wing leveller or autopilot, if equipped, before reducing AOA.
notes.explanation: The handbook ties the disconnect to the moment before AOA is reduced.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot, if equipped, prior to reducing AOA.

notes.front: Which stall-recovery error is about not appreciating what matters most in the recovery?
notes.back: Attempting recovery without recognising the importance of pitch control and AOA.
notes.explanation: The handbook pairs pitch control with AOA, rather than with bank or power, as what the recovery must recognise.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Recovery is attempted without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA.

notes.front: A stall-recovery error is not maintaining a nose-down control input until the {{c1::stall warning is eliminated}}.
notes.back: stall warning is eliminated
notes.explanation: The end point is the warning going away, not a set time or attitude.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Not maintaining a nose down control input until the stall warning is eliminated.

notes.front: Which stall-recovery error puts the throttle ahead of reducing AOA?
notes.back: Attempting to recover with power before reducing AOA.
notes.explanation: It sits between the wings-first error and the failure to roll wings level; all three turn on reducing AOA first.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Pilot attempts to level the wings before reducing AOA. 13. Pilot attempts to recover with power before reducing AOA. 14. Failure to roll wings level after AOA reduction and stall warning is eliminated.

notes.front: Which stall-recovery error produces a second stall?
notes.back: An inadvertent secondary stall during recovery.
notes.explanation: The list follows it with the opposite excess, too much forward-elevator pressure.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Inadvertent secondary stall during recovery. 16. Excessive forward-elevator pressure during recovery resulting in low or negative G load.

notes.front: What does excessive forward-elevator pressure during stall recovery result in?
notes.back: A low or negative G load.
notes.explanation: It is listed right after the secondary stall, the fault at the other end of elevator handling.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Inadvertent secondary stall during recovery. 16. Excessive forward-elevator pressure during recovery resulting in low or negative G load.

notes.front: Which stall-recovery error concerns the speed gained during the recovery?
notes.back: Excessive airspeed buildup.
notes.explanation: It follows excessive forward-elevator pressure on the list.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Excessive forward-elevator pressure during recovery resulting in low or negative G load. 17. Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery.

notes.front: Which final intentional-stall error does the handbook tie to losing situational awareness?
notes.back: Failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions.
notes.explanation: The last item moves past the stall itself to what the pilot does once flying again.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Losing situational awareness and failing to return to desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions.

notes.front: In an intentional spin entry, which rudder error does the handbook list?
notes.back: Not applying full rudder (to the stops) in the desired spin direction.
notes.explanation: The handbook specifies full rudder “to the stops”, so partial rudder counts as the error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Common errors in the performance of intentional spins are: 1. Failure to apply full rudder pressure (to the stops) in the desired spin direction during spin entry

notes.front: In a spin entry, what does failing to apply and hold full up-elevator pressure result in?
notes.back: A spiral.
notes.explanation: The list names the result inside the error: without full up-elevator the entry becomes a spiral, not a spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to apply and maintain full up-elevator pressure during spin entry, resulting in a spiral

notes.front: Which spin-entry error concerns the stall itself?
notes.back: Not achieving a fully stalled condition before spin entry.
notes.explanation: It is the entry error about the stall itself rather than a control input.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to achieve a fully-stalled condition prior to spin entry

notes.front: In spin recovery, which rudder error does the handbook list?
notes.back: Not applying full rudder (to the stops) briskly against the spin.
notes.explanation: The handbook asks for full rudder, briskly and against the spin, so each of those words marks a way to get it wrong.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to apply full rudder (to the stops) briskly against the spin during recovery

notes.front: Which spin-recovery error concerns the amount of forward-elevator?
notes.back: Applying insufficient forward-elevator.
notes.explanation: The next item on the list is about its timing, which is a separate fault.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to apply sufficient forward-elevator during recovery 6. Waiting for rotation to stop before applying forward-elevator

notes.front: Which spin-recovery error concerns when forward-elevator is applied?
notes.back: Waiting for rotation to stop before applying it.
notes.explanation: The list keeps timing apart from amount: enough forward-elevator applied too late is still an error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to apply sufficient forward-elevator during recovery 6. Waiting for rotation to stop before applying forward-elevator

notes.front: What may happen if the rudder is not neutralised after spin rotation stops?
notes.back: A secondary spin.
notes.explanation: The handbook hedges it: failing to neutralise is “possibly resulting in” a secondary spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to neutralize the rudder after rotation stops, possibly resulting in a secondary spin

notes.front: Which spin-recovery error describes the pace of the control movements?
notes.back: Slow and overly cautious control movements.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists the pace of the inputs as a fault in its own right, apart from which controls are used.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Slow and overly cautious control movements during recovery

notes.front: What is the first common error the handbook lists for recovery from a spiral dive?
notes.back: Failing to reduce power first.
notes.explanation: The next item is the reverse fault, mistakenly adding power.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: Failure to reduce power first 2. Mistakenly adding power 3. Attempting to pull out of dive without rolling wings level 4. Simultaneously pulling out of dive while rolling wings level

notes.front: Which spiral-dive recovery error is the opposite of the correct first throttle action?
notes.back: Mistakenly adding power.
notes.explanation: The list opens with failing to reduce power first, then names adding power as its own fault.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: Failure to reduce power first 2. Mistakenly adding power 3. Attempting to pull out of dive without rolling wings level 4. Simultaneously pulling out of dive while rolling wings level

notes.front: Which spiral-dive recovery error pulls out of the dive with no attempt to level the wings?
notes.back: Attempting to pull out without rolling wings level.
notes.explanation: The next item is the half-way version: pulling out while rolling level at the same time.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: Failure to reduce power first 2. Mistakenly adding power 3. Attempting to pull out of dive without rolling wings level 4. Simultaneously pulling out of dive while rolling wings level

notes.front: Which spiral-dive recovery error merges the pull-out and the roll to wings level into one movement?
notes.back: Pulling out of the dive while simultaneously rolling wings level.
notes.explanation: It differs from the previous item because the wings are being levelled, just not before the pull.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: Failure to reduce power first 2. Mistakenly adding power 3. Attempting to pull out of dive without rolling wings level 4. Simultaneously pulling out of dive while rolling wings level

notes.front: Which spiral-dive recovery error concerns G-load before the roll?
notes.back: Not unloading the Gs before rolling level.
notes.explanation: The list ties the unloading to the moment before rolling level, not to the pull-out.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: Not unloading the Gs prior to rolling level 6. Not adding power once climb is established

notes.front: Which spiral-dive recovery error comes at the end, once a climb is established?
notes.back: Not adding power.
notes.explanation: The list faults power at both ends of the recovery: failing to reduce it first and failing to add it once climbing.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-27
notes.evidence: Failure to reduce power first 2. Mistakenly adding power 3. Attempting to pull out of dive without rolling wings level 4. Simultaneously pulling out of dive while rolling wings level 5. Not unloading the Gs prior to rolling level 6. Not adding power once climb is established

notes.front: In spiral-dive recovery, why unload the G-load before rolling the wings level?
notes.back: The airplane’s design limit is exceeded more easily during a rolling pullout.
notes.explanation: Skipping the unload risks structural damage or failure, which the handbook gives as the consequence.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: The design limit of the airplane is exceeded more easily during a rolling pullout, so failure to reduce the G-load prior to rolling the wings level could result in structural damage or failure.

notes.front: Flying a rectangular course round a field, your learner holds altitude well but starts every corner turn noticeably late. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: A) Failure to execute turns with accurate timing
notes.explanation: The fault is when the turns start, and accurate turn timing is an item on the rectangular-course list.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Rectangular Course”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: Failure to properly divide attention between airplane control and orientation with ground references. 9. Failure to execute turns with accurate timing.
notes.choices:
A) Failure to execute turns with accurate timing
B) Failure to establish a constant, level altitude prior to entry
C) Failure to adequately clear the area
D) Failure to maintain altitude during the manoeuvre
notes.choicesExplained: B: altitude at entry is not the problem; she holds altitude well. C: nothing suggests a missed lookout. D: altitude is being held.

notes.front: Circling a barn in a turn around a point, your learner holds one bank angle all the way round and the track drifts downwind into an uneven circle. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: A) Failure to properly execute constant-radius turns
notes.explanation: The handbook says higher groundspeeds need steeper banks and slower groundspeeds shallower ones, so an unchanging bank will not hold a constant radius in wind.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Turns Around a Point”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: The principles are the same in any turning ground reference maneuver—higher groundspeeds require steeper banks and slower ground speeds require shallower banks.
notes.choices:
A) Failure to properly execute constant-radius turns
B) Failure to adequately clear the area
C) Failure to establish a constant, level altitude prior to entry
D) Failure to apply coordinated aileron and rudder pressure
notes.choicesExplained: B: the lookout is not in question. C: the problem is the ground track, not the entry altitude. D: nothing points to a slip or skid.

notes.front: In S-turns across a road, your learner jerks from one bank into the opposite bank each time she crosses. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: B) Failing to handle the controls smoothly and continuously when transitioning into turns
notes.explanation: The S-turn list ties the smooth-control error to the transitions into turns, which is exactly where the jerk happens.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “S-Turns”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: Failure to manipulate the flight controls in a smooth and continuous manner when transitioning into turns.
notes.choices:
A) Failure to properly assess wind direction
B) Failing to handle the controls smoothly and continuously when transitioning into turns
C) Failure to maintain altitude during the manoeuvre
D) Failure to adequately clear the area
notes.choicesExplained: A: the wind is not described as misjudged. C: no altitude change is described. D: nothing suggests a missed lookout.

notes.front: On eights on pylons, the wingtip reference line creeps ahead of the pylon and your learner presses inside rudder to pull it back. What is the error?
notes.back: C) Incorrect use of the rudder, which should be used only for coordination
notes.explanation: The handbook describes exactly this habit, yawing the wing back with inside rudder, as the most common error in holding a pylon.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Eights on Pylons”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: The most common error in attempting to hold a pylon is incorrect use of the rudder. When the projection of the visual reference line moves forward with respect to the pylon, many pilots tend to apply inside rudder pressure to yaw the wing backward.
notes.choices:
A) Poor choice of pylons
B) Not entering the pylon turns into the wind
C) Incorrect use of the rudder, which should be used only for coordination
D) Failure to time the bank for the turn entry
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pylons themselves are not in question. B: the entry direction is not described. D: the entry is already complete; the problem is holding the pylon.

notes.front: Approaching the first pylon, your learner rolls into the bank so late that the pylon has passed the wingtip reference before the bank is set. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: D) Failure to time the bank so the turn entry is complete with the pylon in position
notes.explanation: The list ties the bank timing to where the pylon is when the entry ends, which is what was missed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Eights on Pylons”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: Failure to time the bank so that the turn entry is completed with the pylon in position.
notes.choices:
A) Excessive gain or loss of altitude
B) Inability to select pivotal altitude
C) Poor choice of pylons
D) Failure to time the bank so the turn entry is complete with the pylon in position
notes.choicesExplained: B: altitude is not what went wrong here. C: the pylon choice is not described as poor. A: no altitude change is described.

notes.front: In a 45° steep turn, your learner rolls into 50°, eases to 40°, then drifts to 55°. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: A) Failure to maintain constant bank angle
notes.explanation: The bank keeps changing, and holding a constant bank angle is a listed steep-turn item.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Steep Turns”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Gaining or losing altitude 4. Failure to maintain constant bank angle
notes.choices:
A) Failure to maintain constant bank angle
B) Attempting to start recovery prematurely
C) Ineffective use of trim
D) Not clearing the area
notes.choicesExplained: B: she has not started the rollout. C: nothing points to trim. D: the lookout is not described.

notes.front: Rolling out of a 360° steep turn, your learner sails 20° past the entry heading before the wings are level. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: C) Failure to stop the turn on the designated heading
notes.explanation: The steep-turn list names the rollout heading as its own error, separate from starting the recovery too soon.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Steep Turns”, p. 10-3
notes.evidence: Attempting to start recovery prematurely 13. Failure to stop the turn on the designated heading
notes.choices:
A) Attempting to start recovery prematurely
B) Ineffective use of power
C) Failure to stop the turn on the designated heading
D) Becoming disoriented
notes.choicesExplained: A: she started late, not early. B: nothing points to power. D: she knows the heading; she just overshoots it.

notes.front: In a steep spiral over a field, your learner keeps one bank angle all the way round and the circle drifts off the field downwind. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: B) Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind
notes.explanation: The handbook corrects for drift by steepening the bank on downwind headings and shallowing it on upwind headings.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Steep Spiral”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: wind drift by steepening the bank on downwind headings and shallowing the bank on upwind headings. During the steep spiral, the pilot should continually correct for any changes in wind direction and velocity to maintain a constant radius.
notes.choices:
A) Ineffective use of trim
B) Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind
C) Poor flight control coordination
D) Becoming disoriented
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing points to trim. D: she knows where the field is; the circle is drifting. C: nothing suggests a slip or skid.

notes.front: In a chandelle, your learner holds the entry bank well past the 90° point and only starts rolling out at about 130°. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: C) Not starting the recovery at the 90° point in the turn
notes.explanation: The chandelle list marks the start of recovery at the 90° point, which she passed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Chandelle”, p. 10-6
notes.evidence: Not starting the recovery at the 90° point in the turn
notes.choices:
A) Levelling the wings prior to the 180° point
B) Initial bank is too steep
C) Not starting the recovery at the 90° point in the turn
D) Allowing the bank angle to increase after initial establishment
notes.choicesExplained: B: the entry bank itself is not described as wrong. A: she is late, not early, with the rollout. D: the bank is held, not increased.

notes.front: Your learner enters a chandelle with a very gentle bank and the airplane stalls before the turn is done. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: A) Initial bank is too shallow, resulting in a stall
notes.explanation: The handbook links a too-shallow initial bank directly to a stall.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Chandelle”, p. 10-6
notes.evidence: Initial bank is too shallow resulting in a stall 3. Initial bank is too steep resulting in failure to gain maximum performance
notes.choices:
A) Initial bank is too shallow, resulting in a stall
B) Initial bank is too steep
C) Pitch attitude is low on recovery
D) Not clearing the area
notes.choicesExplained: B: a steep bank costs performance; it is not the fault described. C: low pitch leaves airspeed well above stall, not a stall. D: nothing suggests a missed lookout.

notes.front: In a lazy eight, your learner’s first loop is wide and tall and the second shallow and cramped. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: C) The manoeuvre is not symmetrical across each 180°
notes.explanation: The two halves differ, and symmetry across each 180° is a listed lazy-eight item.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Lazy Eight”, p. 10-7
notes.evidence: Not clearing the area 2. Maneuver is not symmetrical across each 180°
notes.choices:
A) Control roughness
B) Execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing manoeuvre
C) The manoeuvre is not symmetrical across each 180°
D) Not clearing the area
notes.choicesExplained: A: the inputs are not described as rough. B: both loops include a climb. D: nothing suggests a missed lookout.

notes.front: At the top of each climbing segment of a lazy eight, your learner lets the nose drop quickly through the horizon. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: D) Poor control at the top of each climb segment
notes.explanation: The handbook names the nose falling rapidly through the horizon as the result of poor control at the top of the climb.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Lazy Eight”, p. 10-7
notes.evidence: Poor control at the top of each climb segment resulting in the pitch rapidly falling through the horizon
notes.choices:
A) Gain or loss of altitude at each 180° point
B) Inadequate or improper use of the 45°, 90°, 135° references
C) Ineffective planning
D) Poor control at the top of each climb segment
notes.choicesExplained: A: the fault described is pitch at the top, not altitude at the 180° points. B: no reference problem is described. C: the handbook lists this exact pitch result under control at the top, not planning.

notes.front: Entering slow flight, your learner reduces power but holds the nose where it was, and the airplane begins to lose altitude. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: A) Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
notes.explanation: The handbook ties too little back-elevator pressure during the power reduction to altitude loss.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Slow Flight”, p. 5-12
notes.evidence: Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced, resulting in altitude loss
notes.choices:
A) Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
B) Excessive back-elevator pressure as power is reduced
C) Insufficient right rudder
D) Failure to anticipate AOA changes with flaps
notes.choicesExplained: B: too much back pressure gives a climb, not a descent. C: yaw is not described. D: no flap change is described.

notes.front: At the break of a power-on stall the right wing drops, and your learner at once rolls left with aileron while still holding back pressure. What is the error?
notes.back: D) Trying to control the bank before reducing AOA
notes.explanation: The handbook warns against being tempted to control the bank angle before reducing AOA.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Fundamentals of Stall Recovery”, p. 5-16
notes.evidence: 3. Roll wings level. This orients the lift vector properly for an effective recovery. It is important not to be tempted to control the bank angle prior to reducing AOA.
notes.choices:
A) Recovering before reaching the critical AOA
B) Excessive airspeed buildup
C) Not disconnecting the autopilot
D) Trying to control the bank before reducing AOA
notes.choicesExplained: A: the stall has occurred, so this is not an early recovery. C: no autopilot is involved. B: the airplane is slow, not fast.

notes.front: At the stall your learner pushes the throttle full forward but keeps the yoke back. What is the error?
notes.back: B) Trying to recover with power before reducing AOA
notes.explanation: The handbook says power reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall; reducing AOA is imperative.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Fundamentals of Stall Recovery”, p. 5-16
notes.evidence: Adding power typically reduces the loss of altitude during a stall recovery, but it does not eliminate a stall. The reduction in AOA is imperative.
notes.choices:
A) Failure to roll wings level after the warning stops
B) Trying to recover with power before reducing AOA
C) Excessive forward-elevator pressure
D) Failure to clear the area
notes.choicesExplained: A: the wings are not the issue described. C: she has not pushed at all. D: nothing suggests a missed lookout.

notes.front: Recovering from a full stall, your learner shoves the yoke so far forward that loose items lift off the seat. Which listed error fits best?
notes.back: D) Excessive forward-elevator pressure, giving low or negative G
notes.explanation: The list ties excessive forward-elevator during recovery to a low or negative G load.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Excessive forward-elevator pressure during recovery resulting in low or negative G load.
notes.choices:
A) Inadvertent secondary stall
B) Not maintaining a nose-down input until the warning stops
C) Inadvertent accelerated stall on entry
D) Excessive forward-elevator pressure, giving low or negative G
notes.choicesExplained: A: a secondary stall comes from too little nose-down, not too much. B: she has plenty of nose-down input. C: the problem is in the recovery, not the entry.

notes.front: In a spin recovery, rotation stops but your learner keeps holding full opposite rudder. What may this lead to?
notes.back: B) A secondary spin
notes.explanation: The handbook says failing to neutralise the rudder after rotation stops may result in a secondary spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to neutralize the rudder after rotation stops, possibly resulting in a secondary spin
notes.choices:
A) Excessive airspeed
B) A secondary spin
C) A spiral on entry
D) Failure to reach a full stall
notes.choicesExplained: A: excessive airspeed follows too little back-elevator in recovery. C: a spiral comes from not holding full up-elevator on entry. D: that is an entry error; this is recovery.

notes.front: Entering an intentional spin, your learner applies full rudder but relaxes the back pressure, and the airplane goes into a steepening descending turn instead. What is the error?
notes.back: B) Failing to apply and hold full up-elevator during spin entry
notes.explanation: The handbook ties the loss of full up-elevator on entry to a spiral rather than a spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Failure to apply and maintain full up-elevator pressure during spin entry, resulting in a spiral
notes.choices:
A) Slow and overly cautious recovery inputs
B) Failing to apply and hold full up-elevator during spin entry
C) Waiting for rotation to stop before forward-elevator
D) Excessive back-elevator after rotation stops
notes.choicesExplained: A: this is entry, not recovery. C: this is a recovery error. D: this is a recovery error.

notes.front: Your learner finds herself in a nose-low, steeply banked, accelerating spiral dive. What should she do first?
notes.back: B) Reduce power to idle
notes.explanation: The handbook’s first step is to reduce power to idle, to slow the rate of acceleration.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: 1. Reduce power (throttle) to idle. Immediately reduce power to idle to slow the rate of acceleration.
notes.choices:
A) Roll the wings level
B) Reduce power to idle
C) Pull the nose up to the horizon
D) Add full power
notes.choicesExplained: A: rolling level comes after power is reduced and the wing is unloaded. C: raising the nose comes after the wings are level. D: adding power is a listed error.

notes.front: Startled by a steep nose-down attitude and bank, your learner hauls back on the yoke while rolling the wings level. What does the handbook say this response can cause?
notes.back: A) Loads that can damage the airframe or make it fail
notes.explanation: The handbook describes this exact startled reaction and the aerodynamic loads it can create.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spiral Dive”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: the startled pilot may react by pulling back rapidly on the yoke while simultaneously rolling to wings-level. This response can create aerodynamic loads capable of causing airframe structural damage and/or failure.
notes.choices:
A) Loads that can damage the airframe or make it fail
B) A stall warning with no other effect
C) An inadvertent accelerated stall only
D) A secondary spin
notes.choicesExplained: D: a secondary spin is linked to not neutralising rudder after a spin. B: the handbook describes structural loads, not only a warning. C: the handbook names structural damage or failure as the risk.

notes.front: Steep turn or steep spiral: whose handbook common-error list includes ineffective use of power?
notes.back: The steep turn’s; the steep-spiral list has no power item.
notes.explanation: The steep-spiral list names trim and airspeed control but not power.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Steep Spiral”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: Poor flight control coordination 5. Ineffective use of trim 6. Inadequate airspeed control 7. Becoming disoriented

notes.front: Eights on pylons: what rudder errors do pilots make when the reference line moves ahead of the pylon, and when it moves behind?
notes.back: Ahead: inside rudder to yaw the wing back. Behind: outside rudder to yaw it forward. Both are wrong.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the rudder should be used only for coordination, whichever way the line moves.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 7 “Ground Reference Maneuvers”, “Eights on Pylons”, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: When the projection of the visual reference line moves forward with respect to the pylon, many pilots tend to apply inside rudder pressure to yaw the wing backward. When the reference line moves behind the pylon, pilots tend to apply outside rudder pressure to yaw the wing forward. The pilot should use the rudder only for coordination.

notes.front: In spin recovery, how do the results of too much and too little back-elevator pressure differ?
notes.back: Too much after rotation stops may cause a secondary stall; too little gives excessive airspeed.
notes.explanation: The two are the last items on the handbook’s spin list, the two ends of the same control.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Spins”, p. 5-26
notes.evidence: Excessive back-elevator pressure after rotation stops, possibly resulting in secondary stall 10. Insufficient back-elevator pressure during recovery resulting in excessive airspeed

notes.front: In stall recovery, what are the two opposite wing-levelling errors the handbook lists?
notes.back: Levelling the wings before reducing AOA; failing to roll wings level after AOA is reduced and the warning is gone.
notes.explanation: Both errors turn on the order of actions: reduce AOA first, then roll level.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 5 “Maintaining Aircraft Control: Upset Prevention and Recovery Training”, “Stalls: Common Errors”, p. 5-21
notes.evidence: Pilot attempts to level the wings before reducing AOA. 13. Pilot attempts to recover with power before reducing AOA. 14. Failure to roll wings level after AOA reduction and stall warning is eliminated.

notes.front: In a chandelle entry, how do the results of a too-shallow and a too-steep initial bank differ?
notes.back: Too shallow ends in a stall; too steep fails to gain maximum performance.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists both entry-bank faults side by side, with their results.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 10 “Performance Maneuvers”, “Chandelle”, p. 10-6
notes.evidence: Initial bank is too shallow resulting in a stall 3. Initial bank is too steep resulting in failure to gain maximum performance

notes.front: In the region of normal command, what must the pilot do with power to increase speed?
notes.back: Add power.
notes.explanation: This is the familiar region, above the minimum drag point, where more power simply means more speed.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: The “region of normal command” occurs where power must

notes.front: On which side of the minimum drag point does the region of reversed command lie?
notes.back: The slow side: at speeds slower than the minimum drag point.
notes.explanation: The minimum drag point divides the curve; the normal region lies at higher speeds and the reversed region at lower ones.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: region exists at speeds slower than the minimum drag point

notes.front: The region of reversed command exists primarily because of {{c1::induced}} drag.
notes.back: induced
notes.explanation: At the slow point on the curve, induced drag is high and parasite drag low.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: primarily due to induced drag. Figure 4-10 shows how one

notes.front: One power setting can give two level-flight speeds. What is the drag at the slower of the two?
notes.back: High induced drag and low parasite drag.
notes.explanation: At the faster point the balance is reversed: high parasite drag and low induced drag, for the same total power.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: because at point 1 there is high induced drag and low parasite

notes.front: In which phases of flight may the region of reversed command be met?
notes.back: The slow-speed phases of flight during takeoff and landing.
notes.explanation: Most flying, such as cruise, climb and manoeuvres, is done in the region of normal command.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: reversed command may be encountered in the slow-speed

notes.front: For most general aviation aircraft, the region of reversed command is very small and lies below normal {{c1::approach}} speeds.
notes.back: approach
notes.explanation: The handbook still places it in the slow-speed phases of takeoff and landing.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command, page 4-7
notes.evidence: is very small and is below normal approach speeds.

notes.front: Does flight in the region of reversed command mean great control difficulty and danger?
notes.back: Not necessarily; but it amplifies errors of basic flying technique.
notes.explanation: That is why the handbook stresses proper technique and precise control there.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command and Speed Stability, page 4-8
notes.evidence: However, it does amplify errors of basic flying technique—

notes.front: In steady level flight in the region of reversed command, what happens if the aircraft slows below its trimmed point with power unchanged?
notes.back: A power deficiency exists and it tends to keep slowing to an even lower airspeed.
notes.explanation: Excess or deficient power on either side of that point magnifies the original speed change: the speed instability of this region.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command and Speed Stability, page 4-8
notes.evidence: continue to slow to an even lower airspeed.

notes.front: In the flight instructor certification standards (Task X.B), what role does the minimum power required speed play?
notes.back: It separates the region of normal command from the region of reversed command on the power-required curve.
notes.explanation: The instructor applicant must be able to explain this boundary as part of the flight characteristics demonstration.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Knowledge, page 65
notes.evidence: The minimum power required speed and its role in differentiating the region of normal command and the region of reversed command on the power-required curve.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A learner flying level well below normal approach speed lets the airspeed sag a few knots and leaves the power alone. What does the power-required curve predict?
notes.back: A) The aeroplane keeps slowing to an even lower airspeed.
notes.choices:
A) The aeroplane keeps slowing to an even lower airspeed
B) It settles at the new, slightly lower speed
C) It returns by itself to the trimmed speed
D) It speeds up because drag falls as it slows
notes.choicesExplained: C: returning to the trim speed is the region of normal command. B: in this region the speed change is magnified, not held. D: below the minimum drag point, slowing raises drag, leaving a power deficiency.
notes.explanation: Below the trimmed point a power deficiency exists, so the natural tendency is to slow to an even lower airspeed.
notes.source: Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B), Chapter 4, Regions of Command and Speed Stability, page 4-8
notes.evidence: slowed to some airspeed lower than point B, a deficiency

notes.front: What does Task X.B of the flight instructor certification standards, Demonstration of Flight Characteristics at Various Configurations and Airspeeds, test the applicant understands?
notes.back: Flight characteristics and power required at different airspeeds and configurations, for the make and model flown.
notes.explanation: Its knowledge elements include power required and the regions of normal and reversed command.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, page 65
notes.evidence: understands flight characteristics and power required at different airspeeds and configurations appropriate to the make and model of airplane flown
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Across what speed range must the applicant explain power required in Task X.B?
notes.back: From cruise airspeed down to critically slow airspeeds near the critical angle of attack.
notes.explanation: The range spans both regions of command, from normal cruise into the slow end of the curve.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, page 65
notes.evidence: Power required at various airspeeds between cruise airspeed and critically slow airspeeds near the critical angle of attack.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The flight characteristics demonstration must be performed no lower than {{c1::1,500}} feet above ground level.
notes.explanation: The applicant selects an altitude that allows the whole manoeuvre above this floor.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the flight characteristics demonstration, airspeed must be held within {{c1::+5/−0}} knots.
notes.explanation: Altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10° and bank ±5° complete the tolerances.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: maintaining altitude ±100 feet, airspeed +5/-0 knots, heading ±10°, and specified bank angle ±5°
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At what airspeed does the clean configuration demonstration begin?
notes.back: Design/operating manoeuvring speed appropriate to the aeroplane’s weight, while describing pitch, power and trim.
notes.explanation: Starting fast lets the applicant show how pitch, power and trim change as the aeroplane is slowed.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: Establish and maintain design/operating maneuvering speed appropriate to the airplane’s weight while describing pitch, power, and trim inputs
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the clean demonstration, after the starting speed, to what airspeed is the aeroplane slowed first, and what is noted?
notes.back: Best glide speed (or as the evaluator specifies), noting the power setting required.
notes.explanation: The next step slows further, to the speed just short of an immediate stall, again noting power.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: slow the airplane to, and maintain, best glide speed (or as specified by evaluator), noting the power setting required
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does Task X.B define the slowest airspeed to be held in level flight?
notes.back: One at which any further increase in angle of attack or load factor, or reduction in power, would cause an immediate stall.
notes.explanation: The applicant holds it in level flight, noting airspeed and power, while verbally acknowledging the stall warnings.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: an airspeed at which any further increase in angle of attack, increase in load factor, or reduction in power would result in an immediate stall
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does the applicant leave the slowest airspeed at the end of the clean demonstration?
notes.back: Without changing power, lowers the pitch attitude and accelerates to level flight, noting the new airspeed and altitude lost.
notes.explanation: The new airspeed and the altitude lost are noted before returning to cruise.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: Without changing power setting, lower the pitch attitude and accelerate to a faster airspeed until reestablishing the airplane in level flight
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the landing configuration demonstration, with gear and flaps fully extended, to what airspeed is the aeroplane first slowed?
notes.back: Reference landing speed (or as the evaluator specifies), noting the power setting required.
notes.explanation: The landing sequence mirrors the clean one, with reference landing speed taking the place of best glide speed.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: slow the airplane to, and maintain, reference landing speed (or as specified by the evaluator), noting the power setting required
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Task X.B asks for airspeeds specific to the aeroplane. What are two of them, among others?
notes.back: Two among others: best glide speed; reference landing speed.
notes.explanation: The list also names manoeuvring, gear, flap and stalling speeds; the applicant says how to find each on the airspeed indicator.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, page 65
notes.evidence: Airspeeds specific to the airplane for various operations, how to identify them on the airspeed indicator
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In Tasks X.A and X.B, is a momentary stall horn caused by turbulence unsatisfactory?
notes.back: No, if the applicant recognises it and promptly corrects.
notes.explanation: Unsatisfactory performance is continual deviation, lack of correction or lack of recognition.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix 3, Area of Operation X, page 103
notes.evidence: If the applicant recognizes the stall warning indication and promptly makes an appropriate correction, a momentary activation does not constitute unsatisfactory performance on this Task.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: During a practice demonstration, an applicant at the slowest level-flight airspeed adds power as they lower the nose to accelerate. What has the applicant missed?
notes.back: C) Power is left unchanged while the nose is lowered to accelerate.
notes.choices:
A) Power should be cut to idle before lowering the nose
B) The nose should be raised to regain altitude first
C) Power is left unchanged while the nose is lowered to accelerate
D) Flaps should be retracted before any acceleration
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Task holds power where it was; idle is not asked for. B: raising the nose at that speed would cause an immediate stall. D: the clean demonstration has no flaps to retract, and the Task says nothing of it.
notes.explanation: The Task says to lower the pitch and accelerate without changing the power setting, noting the new airspeed and altitude lost.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task B, Skills, page 66
notes.evidence: Without changing power setting, lower the pitch attitude and accelerate to a faster airspeed until reestablishing the airplane in level flight
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the objective of the cross-control stall demonstration?
notes.back: To show how uncoordinated flight affects stall behaviour and stress coordinated flight in turns.
notes.explanation: All pilots should know how to recognise, avoid and recover from this stall.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: to show the effects of uncoordinated flight on stall behavior and to emphasize the importance of maintaining coordinated flight while making turns

notes.front: Who may be required to perform the cross-control stall on a practical test?
notes.back: Only flight instructor applicants; it is a demonstration-only manoeuvre.
notes.explanation: All pilots should still know the situations that lead to it and how to recognise, avoid and recover from it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: This is a demonstration-only maneuver; only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform it on a practical test.

notes.front: What control inputs are present in a cross-control stall?
notes.back: Critical angle of attack exceeded with aileron pressure one way and rudder pressure the opposite way.
notes.explanation: Opposing aileron and rudder is what makes the flight uncoordinated.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: A cross-control stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded with aileron pressure applied in one direction and rudder pressure in the opposite direction

notes.front: Where is a skidding cross-control stall most likely to occur?
notes.back: In the traffic pattern, during a poorly planned and executed base-to-final turn.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns that this stall can be deadly if it occurs close to the ground.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: A skidding cross-control stall is most likely to occur in the traffic pattern during a poorly planned and executed base-to-final approach turn.

notes.front: In the handbook’s account of a skidding cross-control stall, what may cause the late or shallow turn to final?
notes.back: An unrecognised tailwind component and higher groundspeed on the base leg.
notes.explanation: The late turn leads to an overshoot, which tempts the pilot to add bank, back pressure and inside rudder.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: There may be an unrecognized tailwind component and higher groundspeed on the base leg, which causes the pilot to turn late or with inadequate bank.

notes.front: Having overshot final, what three inputs does the pilot make in the classic skidding cross-control scenario?
notes.back: More bank, more back elevator pressure, and excess rudder toward the turn (inside or bottom rudder).
notes.explanation: The rudder is used to swing the nose round to the runway, setting up the cross-control.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: increasing the bank angle, increasing back elevator pressure, and applying excess rudder in the direction of the turn (i.e., inside or bottom rudder pressure)

notes.front: What may the aeroplane do when a cross-control stall occurs?
notes.back: Pitch down, change bank suddenly, and keep rolling towards inverted, usually the beginning of a spin.
notes.explanation: It can come with very little warning, which is why it can be deadly close to the ground.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: The nose may pitch down, the bank angle may suddenly change, and the airplane may continue to roll to an inverted orientation, which is usually the beginning of a spin.

notes.front: What does the handbook call the safest action for an overshoot of the turn to final?
notes.back: A go-around.
notes.explanation: Tightening the turn near the ground is how the skidding cross-control stall starts.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: The safest action for an “overshoot” is to perform a go-around.

notes.front: At the low altitude of a base-to-final turn, a pilot should be reluctant to use bank angles greater than {{c1::30}} degrees.
notes.explanation: The handbook pairs this with never making a skidding turn to correct an overshoot.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: a pilot should be reluctant to use bank angles greater than 30 degrees and should not make a skidding turn

notes.front: Why are the flaps left up for the cross-control stall demonstration?
notes.back: To avoid the possibility of exceeding the aeroplane’s limitations.
notes.explanation: The gear is lowered and the throttle closed, but flaps stay retracted.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: To avoid the possibility of exceeding the airplane’s limitations, the pilot should not extend the flaps.

notes.front: In the medium-banked gliding turn of the cross-control demonstration, what control pressures are applied?
notes.back: Excess rudder towards the turn, opposite aileron to hold the bank, and back elevator to stop the nose lowering.
notes.explanation: All three pressures are increased together until the aeroplane stalls.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: the pilot should smoothly apply excessive rudder pressure in the direction of the turn and hold the bank constant by applying opposite aileron pressure

notes.front: How does the pilot recover from the cross-control stall demonstration?
notes.back: Nose-down elevator until the stall warning goes, remove the excess rudder and level the wings, then add power as needed.
notes.explanation: The angle of attack is reduced before the wings are levelled.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: the pilot applies nose-down elevator pressure to reduce the AOA until the stall warning has been eliminated, removes the excessive rudder input and levels the wings, and adds power as needed

notes.front: Task X.F of the flight instructor certification standards requires an entry altitude that lets the cross-controlled stall be completed no lower than {{c1::3,000}} feet AGL.
notes.explanation: The same floor applies to the elevator trim and secondary stall demonstrations.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task F, Skills, page 71
notes.evidence: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a solo check, a learner with a tailwind on base overshoots the extended centreline and starts pushing the inside rudder to swing the nose round. What should the instructor have them do?
notes.back: C) Go around.
notes.choices:
A) Keep the rudder in and add back pressure
B) Steepen the bank past 45° to tighten the turn
C) Go around
D) Add opposite aileron to hold the bank
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook says to be reluctant to exceed 30° of bank in this turn. A: back pressure with bottom rudder is the cross-control stall set-up. D: rudder one way and aileron the other is the cross-control itself.
notes.explanation: The handbook names a go-around as the safest action for an overshoot and warns against a skidding turn to correct it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Cross-Control Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: The safest action for an “overshoot” is to perform a go-around.

notes.front: What does the elevator trim stall demonstration show?
notes.back: What can happen when the pilot applies full power for a go-around without keeping positive control.
notes.explanation: Like the cross-control stall, it is demonstration-only and only instructor applicants may be required to perform it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-20
notes.evidence: The elevator trim stall demonstration shows what can happen when the pilot applies full power for a go-around without maintaining positive control of the airplane.

notes.front: In what situations may an elevator trim stall occur?
notes.back: A go-around from a normal or simulated forced-landing approach, or just after takeoff, with trim set for the approach glide.
notes.explanation: The common element is nose-up approach trim meeting full power.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: during a go-around procedure from a normal landing approach or a simulated, forced-landing approach, or immediately after a takeoff, with the trim set for a normal landing approach glide at idle power

notes.front: The elevator trim stall demonstration shows the importance of what? Name two.
notes.back: Two among others: smooth power application; overcoming strong trim forces.
notes.explanation: The handbook also names positive control to hold safe attitudes and proper, timely trim.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: The demonstration shows the importance of making smooth power applications, overcoming strong trim forces, maintaining positive control of the airplane to hold safe flight attitudes, and using proper and timely trim techniques.

notes.front: How far are the flaps extended for the elevator trim stall demonstration?
notes.back: To the one-half or full position.
notes.explanation: This contrasts with the cross-control demonstration, where the flaps stay up.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: The next step is to extend the flaps to the one-half or full position

notes.front: Once the normal glide is established in the elevator trim stall demonstration, how is the aeroplane trimmed?
notes.back: Nose-up, for the normal landing approach glide.
notes.explanation: Together with propwash over the tail, this trim makes the nose rise sharply when power is added.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: the pilot should trim the airplane nose-up for the normal landing approach glide

notes.front: During the simulated final approach glide, how is the throttle used to set up the elevator trim stall?
notes.back: Advanced smoothly to maximum allowable power, as for a go-around.
notes.explanation: The Task simulates the moment of a real go-around.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: the throttle is then advanced smoothly to maximum allowable power, just as it would be adjusted to perform a go-around

notes.front: When full power is applied with approach trim set, what does the nose tend to do, and why?
notes.back: Rise sharply and turn left, from propwash over the tail combined with elevator trim.
