notes.explanation: Pitch then climbs above the normal climbing attitude if the pilot does not hold it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: The combined effects of increased propwash over the tail and elevator trim tend to make the nose rise sharply and turn to the left.

notes.front: As the elevator trim stall approaches, what should the pilot do?
notes.back: Apply enough forward elevator to reduce angle of attack and stop the stall warning, then return to the normal climb attitude and retrim.
notes.explanation: Retrimming relieves the heavy control pressures so the go-around can be completed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: the pilot should apply sufficient forward elevator pressure to reduce the AOA and eliminate the stall warning before returning the airplane to the normal climbing attitude

notes.front: If the elevator trim stall is taken to a full stall, what will recovery require?
notes.back: A significant nose-down attitude and a corresponding significant loss of altitude.
notes.explanation: The angle of attack must be brought below critical from a steep nose-high state.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: recovery will require a significant nose-down attitude to reduce the AOA below its critical AOA, along with a corresponding significant loss of altitude

notes.front: According to Appendix 3 of the flight instructor certification standards, what must happen before an elevator trim stall is executed, and what is a realistic set-up?
notes.back: The recovery is briefed first; a simulated short-field approach at altitude, trimmed for approach speed, low power, full flaps.
notes.explanation: Appendix 3 sets this for Task G, the elevator trim stall demonstration.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix 3, Task G, page 104
notes.evidence: The applicant and evaluator must brief the recovery prior to stall execution. A realistic scenario includes a simulated
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A learner rejects a landing, shoves the throttle fully forward and relaxes the yoke; the nose rears up and yaws left and the stall horn sounds. What input comes first?
notes.back: C) Forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack.
notes.choices:
A) Full right aileron to level the wings
B) Retract the flaps fully at once
C) Forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack
D) Nose-down trim, and only then any elevator input
notes.choicesExplained: A: rolling does not reduce the angle of attack. B: the handbook’s recovery says nothing of dumping flaps. D: trim is adjusted after the forward elevator has reduced the angle of attack, to relieve the pressure.
notes.explanation: The handbook recovery applies forward elevator to reduce angle of attack and stop the stall warning, and only then adjusts trim.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Elevator Trim Stall, page 5-21
notes.evidence: the pilot should apply sufficient forward elevator pressure to reduce the AOA and eliminate the stall warning

notes.front: Why is a secondary stall so named?
notes.back: Because it occurs after recovery from a preceding stall.
notes.explanation: It is a second stall caused during the recovery from the first.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Secondary Stall, page 5-18
notes.evidence: A secondary stall is so named because it occurs after recovery from a preceding stall.

notes.front: After a stall at low altitude, what is the pilot’s natural impulse that sets up a secondary stall?
notes.back: To bring the nose up as soon as possible, and abruptly.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that this reaction grows stronger the nearer the ground is.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Secondary Stall, page 5-18
notes.evidence: the pilot's natural impulse is to bring the nose up as soon as possible and to do so abruptly

notes.front: How is a secondary stall demonstrated at altitude?
notes.back: Make an abrupt recovery after one stall, exceeding the critical angle of attack a second time.
notes.explanation: Doing it high shows the learner what the low-altitude impulse would cause.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Secondary Stall, page 5-18
notes.evidence: the pilot makes an abrupt recovery after one stall and exceeds the critical AOA a second time

notes.front: Besides an abrupt pull-up, what two recovery faults can cause a secondary stall?
notes.back: Not lowering the pitch enough to reduce angle of attack; trying to break the stall with power only.
notes.explanation: The handbook says this stall may follow any stall recovered in these ways.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Secondary Stall, page 5-18
notes.evidence: when the pilot does not sufficiently reduce the AOA by lowering the pitch attitude or attempts to break the stall by using power only

notes.front: If a secondary stall occurs, how does the pilot recover?
notes.back: Repeat the stall recovery: nose-down elevator to stop the warning, level the wings, coordinate with rudder, adjust power.
notes.explanation: Once no longer stalled, the pilot returns to the desired flightpath.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Secondary Stall, page 5-19
notes.evidence: the pilot should again perform the stall recovery procedures by applying nose-down elevator pressure as required to eliminate the stall warning, level the wings with ailerons, coordinate with rudder, and adjust power as needed

notes.front: Unlike most stall Tasks, may the evaluator ask for recovery at the first indication in the secondary stall Task?
notes.back: No; secondary stalls include a full stall.
notes.explanation: For the other stall Tasks, except the accelerated stall, the evaluator chooses first indication or full stall.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix 3, Area of Operation X, page 103
notes.evidence: With the exception of Task H - Secondary Stalls (where a full stall occurs)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Why does a flight instructor normally demonstrate the cross-controlled, elevator trim and secondary stalls to learners?
notes.back: For familiarisation and stall/spin awareness; private and commercial certification do not include these Tasks.
notes.explanation: Learners see them demonstrated rather than being tested on them.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix 3, Area of Operation X, page 103
notes.evidence: The flight instructor normally demonstrates stall Tasks F, G, and H to learners for the purposes of familiarization and stall/ spin awareness.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Recovering from a power-off stall, a learner adds full power but keeps the nose at the stalled pitch attitude. The buffet returns. What has happened?
notes.back: A) A secondary stall, from trying to break the stall with power alone.
notes.choices:
A) A secondary stall, from trying to break the stall with power alone
B) An elevator trim stall from nose-up trim
C) An accelerated stall from excess bank
D) A cross-control stall from rudder use
notes.choicesExplained: C: nothing in the recovery added bank or G-load. B: an elevator trim stall comes from trim forces on a go-around, not a held attitude. D: no aileron and rudder were crossed.
notes.explanation: The handbook names using power only, without lowering the pitch, as a way to meet a secondary stall.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Secondary Stall, page 5-18
notes.evidence: or attempts to break the stall by using power only

notes.front: What is the first rule for spin demonstration?
notes.back: Make sure the aeroplane is approved for spins.
notes.explanation: The handbook follows it with a review of the flight manual and regulations before any spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: The first rule for spin demonstration is to ensure that the airplane is approved for spins.

notes.front: Before spins, which parts of the aeroplane’s paperwork show whether it is approved for spins?
notes.back: The flight manual’s limitations section, placards, or type certification data.
notes.explanation: This is the first item of the handbook’s pre-spin review.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: The airplane’s AFM/POH limitations section, placards, or type certification data to determine if the airplane is approved for spins

notes.front: Which regulatory requirement does the handbook’s pre-spin review include?
notes.back: The current part 91 parachute requirements.
notes.explanation: The review also covers weight and balance limits and the recommended entry and recovery procedures.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: The current 14 CFR part 91 parachute requirements

notes.front: Besides approval, limits and parachutes, what procedures does the pre-spin review of the flight manual cover?
notes.back: The recommended entry and recovery procedures.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s generic procedures do not replace a particular aeroplane’s own.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: Recommended entry and recovery procedures

notes.front: Which loading item is on the handbook’s pre-spin review list?
notes.back: Weight and balance limitations.
notes.explanation: Loading can change how an aeroplane spins and recovers, as the handbook explains later.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: Weight and balance limitations

notes.front: Why does the pre-spin preflight inspection check for slack or loose control cables?
notes.back: They could prevent full anti-spin control deflection and delay or prevent recovery in some aeroplanes.
notes.explanation: Rudder and elevator cables are the handbook’s particular concern.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: Slack or loose control cables (particularly rudder and elevator) could prevent full anti-spin control deflections and delay or preclude recovery in some airplanes.

notes.front: If the manufacturer does not specifically approve an aircraft for spins, are intentional spins allowed?
notes.back: No; they are not authorised by the regulations or suggested by the handbook.
notes.explanation: Approval must come from the manufacturer’s official sources, not from the pilot’s reasoning.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: If the manufacturer does not specifically approve an aircraft for spins, intentional spins are not authorized by the CFRs or suggested by this handbook.

notes.front: Which certification document is an official source for whether spins are approved?
notes.back: The Type Certificate Data Sheets or the aircraft specifications.
notes.explanation: The other official sources are the flight manual’s limitations section and a placard in view of the pilot.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: Type Certificate Data Sheets or the aircraft specifications

notes.front: Where in the cockpit may spin approval, or its prohibition, be shown?
notes.back: On a placard in clear view of the pilot.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s example placard says that no acrobatic manoeuvres, spins included, are approved.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: On a placard located in clear view of the pilot in the airplane

notes.front: In an aeroplane placarded against spins, is recovery from a fully developed spin assured?
notes.back: No; there is no assurance it is possible.
notes.explanation: The pilot should assume such an aeroplane could become uncontrollable in a spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: In airplanes placarded against spins, there is no assurance that recovery from a fully-developed spin is possible.

notes.front: Under section 23.221(a) of the part 23 certification rules, what spin recovery did normal category single-engine certification require (unless spin resistance was shown)?
notes.back: Recovery from a one-turn or three-second spin, whichever is longer, within one additional turn.
notes.explanation: So many such aeroplanes were never required to recover from a fully developed spin.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: only required the airplane to recover from a one-turn spin or a three-second spin, whichever takes longer, in not more than one additional turn

notes.front: What rationalisation do some pilots, and even instructors, use to justify spinning aeroplanes placarded against it?
notes.back: That the restriction is a "technicality" in the airworthiness standards.
notes.explanation: They reason that spin testing during certification means no problem should arise, overlooking how limited that testing was.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: rationalizing that the spin restriction results from a “technicality” in the airworthiness standards

notes.front: A colleague plans to show a learner a two-turn spin in a trainer placarded against spins, saying "it was spin-tested for certification, so it’s fine". What is the right response?
notes.back: B) Do not spin it: the aeroplane is not approved for spins.
notes.choices:
A) Proceed, but limit it to two turns
B) Do not spin it: the aeroplane is not approved for spins
C) Proceed if entry is above 4,000 feet
D) Proceed if both wear parachutes
notes.choicesExplained: A: certification may have tested only a one-turn or three-second spin, so two turns is beyond it. D: parachutes do not make an unapproved manoeuvre authorised. C: altitude does not change the aeroplane’s approval.
notes.explanation: The first rule is that the aeroplane must be approved for spins; without the manufacturer’s approval, intentional spins are not authorised.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: If the manufacturer does not specifically approve an aircraft for spins, intentional spins are not authorized by the CFRs

notes.front: Can minor weight or balance changes affect an approved aeroplane’s spin recovery?
notes.back: Yes; even minor changes can degrade or enhance spin and recovery characteristics.
notes.explanation: Compliance with weight and balance is important for safe spins and recovery.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Weight and Balance Requirement Related to Spins, page 5-26
notes.evidence: Pilots should know that even minor weight or balance changes can affect the airplane’s spin recovery characteristics.

notes.front: What example does the handbook give of loading that stays within CG limits yet could seriously affect spin recovery?
notes.back: Adding weight in the aft baggage compartment, or additional fuel.
notes.explanation: Being inside the envelope is not the same as being loaded for spins.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Weight and Balance Requirement Related to Spins, page 5-26
notes.evidence: the addition of weight in the aft baggage compartment, or additional fuel, may still permit the airplane to be operated within CG, but could seriously affect the spin and recovery characteristics

notes.front: Compared with utility category loading, how does normal category loading affect resistance to spin entry?
notes.back: It may lower it: the less restricted aft CG and higher weight give less resistance to spin entry.
notes.explanation: An aeroplane hard to spin in the utility category can spin more readily when loaded to normal category limits.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Weight and Balance Requirement Related to Spins, page 5-26
notes.evidence: could have less resistance to spin entry in the normal category (less restricted aft CG and increased weight)

notes.front: Why can normal category loading reduce an aeroplane’s resistance to spin entry?
notes.back: Because of the aeroplane’s ability to generate a higher angle of attack.
notes.explanation: The handbook ties the reduced resistance to this higher angle of attack.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Weight and Balance Requirement Related to Spins, page 5-26
notes.evidence: This situation arises from the airplane’s ability to generate a higher AOA.

notes.front: An aeroplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded to the normal category may not recover from a spin allowed to progress beyond {{c1::one turn}}.
notes.back: one turn
notes.explanation: The approval belongs to a loading, not just to the aeroplane.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Weight and Balance Requirement Related to Spins, page 5-26
notes.evidence: An airplane that is approved for spins in the utility category but loaded in accordance with the normal category may not recover from a spin that is allowed to progress beyond one turn.

notes.front: Before intentional spins, whose CG limitations must the aeroplane be within?
notes.back: Any CG limitations the manufacturer sets.
notes.explanation: The preflight also looks for loose or excess items that could shift weight and CG.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: It is also important to ensure that the airplane is within any CG limitations as determined by the manufacturer.

notes.front: A trainer is approved for spins in the utility category only. The instructor has filled the aft baggage area and tanks to the normal category limits. What should happen before spin training?
notes.back: A) Reload within utility category limits.
notes.choices:
A) Reload within utility category limits
B) Nothing, provided the CG is within normal category limits
C) Limit the spin to three turns
D) Add power during the recovery
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook warns that loading within CG can still seriously affect spin recovery. C: loaded to normal category, it may not recover beyond one turn. D: power aggravates spin characteristics.
notes.explanation: Spin approval here is for utility category loading; loaded to normal category, recovery beyond one turn may not happen.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Weight and Balance Requirement Related to Spins, page 5-26
notes.evidence: An airplane that is approved for spins in the utility category but loaded in accordance with the normal category may not recover from a spin

notes.front: Under 61.49(b), what must an airplane flight instructor applicant who failed on stall awareness or spins bring to the retest?
notes.back: An aircraft of the right category that is certificated for spins.
notes.explanation: The retest requires a real demonstration of spin instructional proficiency to an examiner.
notes.evidence: Bring an aircraft to the retest that is of the appropriate aircraft category for the rating sought and is certificated for spins
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What may the evaluator accept instead of Task X.I, Spin Awareness and Spins, and who must certify it?
notes.back: A logbook record of spin instructional competency, certified by the instructor who gave the spin instruction.
notes.explanation: Acceptance is at the evaluator’s discretion.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task I, page 73
notes.evidence: a logbook record attesting applicant instructional competency in spin entries, spins, and spin recoveries may be accepted in lieu of this Task
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For Task X.I of the flight instructor certification standards, the entry altitude must let the Task be completed no lower than {{c1::4,000}} feet AGL.
notes.explanation: This is higher than the 3,000 feet AGL floor of the cross-control, elevator trim and secondary stall demonstrations.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task I, Skills, page 74
notes.evidence: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 4,000 feet AGL.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In Task X.I of the flight instructor certification standards, on what two bases must the applicant explain how to tell if an aeroplane is approved for spins?
notes.back: Its airworthiness category and its type certificate.
notes.explanation: This is the certification standards’ counterpart of the handbook’s first rule for spin demonstration.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task I, Knowledge, page 74
notes.evidence: How to determine if an airplane approved for the spin maneuver based on airworthiness category and type certificate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: All spins should begin high enough to complete recovery at or above {{c1::1,500}} feet AGL.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that the area above and below should be cleared first.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: all spins should begin at an altitude high enough to complete recovery at or above 1,500 feet AGL

notes.front: Roughly how much altitude does a spin lose in its first turn and in each later turn?
notes.back: About 1,000 feet in the first turn; about half that in each later turn.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives them right after the rule that recovery be complete at or above 1,500 feet AGL.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: the first turn in a spin results in an altitude loss of approximately 1,000 feet, while each subsequent turn loses about half that amount

notes.front: How may spin training appropriately be introduced?
notes.back: By first practising power-on and power-off stalls in a clean configuration.
notes.explanation: This familiarises the pilot with the aeroplane’s own stall and recovery characteristics.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Spin Procedures, page 5-23
notes.evidence: It may be appropriate to introduce spin training by first practicing both power-on and power-off stalls in a clean configuration.

notes.front: Which spin manoeuvre is most commonly used in initial spin training?
notes.back: Incipient spins not allowed to develop into a steady-state spin.
notes.explanation: Recovery in the incipient phase should start before 360° of rotation.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Incipient Phase, page 5-24
notes.evidence: Incipient spins that are not allowed to develop into a steady-state spin are the most commonly used maneuver in initial spin training

notes.front: During a spin, which instrument indication shows the direction of rotation?
notes.back: The symbolic aeroplane of the turn indicator.
notes.explanation: Task X.I asks which instruments are reliable for spin direction; this is the handbook’s answer.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Incipient Phase, page 5-24
notes.evidence: the symbolic airplane of the turn indicator should indicate the direction of the spin

notes.front: Why should the slip/skid ball not be used to tell spin direction?
notes.back: Its movement depends on where it is mounted, not on the direction of the spin.
notes.explanation: A ball mounted on the left side always moves left, even in a spin to the right.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Incipient Phase, page 5-24
notes.evidence: The location of the instrument in the airplane determines how the ball will move rather than the direction of the spin.

notes.front: In a practice spin, a learner calls "spinning left" because the slip/skid ball on the left of the panel sits hard left. The turn indicator’s symbolic aeroplane shows a right turn. Which way is the spin?
notes.back: D) Right, as the turn indicator shows.
notes.choices:
A) Left, as the ball shows
B) It cannot be told from the instruments
C) Whichever way the heading indicator last moved
D) Right, as the turn indicator shows
notes.choicesExplained: A: the ball’s position depends on where it is mounted, not the spin. B: the turn indicator shows the direction. C: the handbook names the turn indicator, not the heading indicator.
notes.explanation: The symbolic aeroplane of the turn indicator shows spin direction; a left-mounted ball always moves left.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Incipient Phase, page 5-24
notes.evidence: the ball mounted on the left side of the airplane will always move to the left, even in spin with rotation to the right

notes.front: Among Task X.I’s risk elements, which one names human-performance hazards?
notes.back: Distractions, task prioritisation, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation.
notes.explanation: These sit beside the spin recovery procedure, environmental effects and collision hazards.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Area of Operation X, Task I, Risk Management, page 74
notes.evidence: Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What do accident records show about pilots and spin restrictions?
notes.back: Some pilots intentionally ignored spin restrictions.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that placards prohibiting spins did not stop them.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), Chapter 5, Intentional Spins, page 5-25
notes.evidence: Unfortunately, accident records show occurrences in which pilots intentionally ignored spin restrictions.

notes.front: Under Appendix 2 of the flight instructor certification standards, what must applicant and instructor or evaluator always do about stalls and spins during training and testing?
notes.back: Recognise and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin and loss of control.
notes.explanation: This applies throughout, not only in the stall and spin Tasks.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix 2, Stall and Spin Awareness, page 100
notes.evidence: must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin and inadvertent loss of control
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which upset recovery error comes before any control input: getting what wrong?
